The correct answer is **Iltutmish**. He is widely recognized for consolidating the **Delhi Sultanate** by adopting sophisticated **Persian courtly customs** to establish the legitimacy and authority of his rule.

* **Iltutmish** introduced the **Iqta system**, which was a Persian administrative model, and adapted it to manage the vast lands of the Indian subcontinent.
* He fostered a culture of Persian literature and etiquette, effectively blending foreign monarchical traditions with the diverse social fabric of India.

The other options are incorrect because **Diwan-i-Amir kohi** refers to an agricultural department established by Muhammad bin Tughluq. **Ibrahim Lodi** was the final ruler of the Lodi dynasty, known more for his conflict with the Mughals, while **Alauddin Bahman Shah** was the founder of the Bahmani Kingdom in the Deccan, established much later.

Related Facts:
* **Iltutmish** was the first ruler to issue regular silver tanka and copper jital coins.
* He completed the construction of the **Qutb Minar**, showing his commitment to building a lasting Islamic architectural legacy in India.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Who among the following Sultans introduced professional courses in education?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **Firoz Shah Tughlaq**.

**Firoz Shah Tughlaq** was a visionary ruler who significantly contributed to the educational landscape of the **Delhi Sultanate**. He established numerous **madrasas** and schools, and he is specifically recognized for encouraging **vocational training** and professional education to help students earn a livelihood after their studies.

Regarding the other options:
* **Ibrahim Lodi** was the last ruler of the Lodi dynasty and did not focus on educational reforms.
* **Iltutmish** is known for building the **Hauz-i-Shamsi** and strengthening the Sultanate but did not introduce professional courses.
* **Diwan-i-Amir Kohi** is not a person; it is a department of agriculture established by **Muhammad bin Tughlaq**.

**Related Facts:**
* **Firoz Shah Tughlaq** also set up a large number of hospitals known as **Dar-ul-Shifa**.
* He is credited with establishing the city of **Hisar** and **Firozabad**.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Coins of which Muslim ruler has the image of Devi Lakshmi?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **Muhammad Ghori**.

In the history of the **Delhi Sultanate**, **Muhammad Ghori** issued gold coins that featured the image of the Hindu goddess **Devi Lakshmi** on the obverse side.

This decision was a strategic move to facilitate trade and gain acceptance among the local population in the newly conquered territories of Northern India.

The coins were modeled after the design of the **Gahadavala dynasty**, who ruled over Kannauj at that time. By adopting a familiar iconography, Ghori ensured his currency was easily recognized and trusted by his subjects.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

* **Jalal-ud-din** (Khilji) founded the Khilji dynasty much later; his coinage did not feature Hindu deities.
* **Ibrahim Lodi** was the last ruler of the Lodi dynasty and issued standard Islamic-style currency.
* **Diwan-i-Amir kohi** is not a ruler, but rather the name of the **Department of Agriculture** established by **Muhammad bin Tughlaq**.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Which Sultan of Delhi assumed the title of Alexander the Great?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **Alauddin Khilji**. Although the provided list suggests otherwise, historical records confirm that **Alauddin Khilji** was the ruler who assumed the title **Sikandar-i-Sani**, which translates to "the Second Alexander."

**Alauddin Khilji** was the second and most powerful ruler of the **Khilji dynasty**. He harbored grand ambitions of world conquest, inspired by the legendary exploits of **Alexander the Great**.

He struck coins featuring this title to document his aspirations. He successfully expanded the **Delhi Sultanate** deep into Southern India, demonstrating military prowess that matched his ambitious title.

Why the other options do not fit:

* **Iltutmish** was a ruler of the **Slave Dynasty** who consolidated the Sultanate but did not claim the title of Alexander.
* **Sikandar Lodi** was a ruler of the **Lodi Dynasty** known for shifting his capital to **Agra**, but he is not associated with the title of Alexander.
* **Ibrahim Lodi** was the last ruler of the **Lodi Dynasty** and the Sultanate, famously defeated by **Babur** at the **First Battle of Panipat** in 1526.

**Alauddin Khilji** remains the only Sultan in Delhi's history to officially adopt the title of the "Second Alexander."

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Who was the founder of Pushtimarg?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **Vallabhacharya**.

**Vallabhacharya** (1479–1531) was a prominent Hindu philosopher and the founder of the **Pushtimarg** (the path of grace), which is a sub-tradition of the **Vaishnava** sect.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

*   **Madhvacharya** was the founder of the **Dvaita** (dualism) school of philosophy, which emphasizes the distinction between the individual soul and the supreme reality.
*   **Jalal-ud-din** refers to the personal name of emperors like Akbar the Great or the founder of the Khilji dynasty, who were rulers, not religious reformers associated with Pushtimarg.
*   **Ibrahim Lodi** was the final ruler of the **Lodi Dynasty** of the Delhi Sultanate and is known for his defeat in the First Battle of Panipat, not for religious philosophy.

**Pushtimarg** focuses on the path of **Bhakti** (devotion) and centers on the worship of **Shrinathji**, a form of Lord Krishna. It emphasizes that divine grace (*Pushti*) is essential for the attainment of spiritual liberation.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Which one of the following was the first ruler of Vijayanagar to have employed Turkish bowmen?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **Devaraya I**.

Historical records, particularly the accounts of the Italian traveler **Nicolo de Conti**, confirm that **Devaraya I** was the first Vijayanagara ruler to modernize his army by employing **Turkish bowmen**.

He initiated this military reform to counter the superior archery skills of the **Bahmani Sultanate** forces. By recruiting these skilled archers, he aimed to compensate for the limitations of his infantry.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

* **Harihara I and Bukka I**: As the founders of the **Sangama dynasty**, they focused primarily on consolidating the empire and resisting the expansion of the Delhi Sultanate rather than introducing specialized foreign military units.
* **Harihara II**: While he expanded the empire significantly, there is no historical evidence suggesting he initiated the recruitment of Turkish bowmen into the Vijayanagara ranks.

**Devaraya I** is also noted for his emphasis on improving **cavalry** and irrigation works, such as the construction of dams across the **Tungabhadra River**, which significantly boosted the agricultural and military strength of the kingdom.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Who among the following is the author of Siyarul Aulia?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct author of **Siyar-ul-Auliya** is **Sayyid Muhammad Mubarak Kirmani**, who is more commonly known as **Amir Khwurd**.

This literary work is a significant **hagiographical text** that documents the lives and teachings of the **Chishti Sufi saints**, specifically focusing on **Nizamuddin Auliya**.

Here is why the other options provided are incorrect:

* **Iltutmish** was a Sultan of the **Delhi Sultanate** and a prominent political figure, not an author of Sufi hagiographies.
* **Bukka I** was a founding ruler of the **Vijayanagara Empire** and was occupied with military and administrative consolidation in South India.
* **Amir Khusro** was a famous poet and scholar under the Delhi Sultanate, but he is known for his own extensive poetic works, not for writing Siyar-ul-Auliya.

Since the actual author, **Amir Khwurd**, is not listed among the first three options, the correct choice is **None of these**.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Which Sultan of Delhi is said to have adopted the policy of blood and iron?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **Balban**.

The policy of **Blood and Iron** was adopted by **Ghiyas-ud-din Balban**, who ruled the Delhi Sultanate from 1266 to 1287 AD. This policy involved a ruthless approach to governance where the Sultan used strict military force, terror, and harsh punishment to maintain order and suppress rebellions.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

* **Amir Khusro** was a legendary poet, scholar, and musician often called the "Parrot of India." He was a courtier under several Sultans but was not a ruler himself.
* **Iltutmish** was a prominent Sultan known for consolidating the Sultanate and establishing the **Iqta system**, but he did not follow the specific policy of Blood and Iron.
* **Ibrahim Lodi** was the last Sultan of the Lodi dynasty and the Delhi Sultanate. He was defeated by Babur in the First Battle of Panipat in 1526 AD.

**Balban** implemented this harsh policy to restore the prestige of the crown. He believed that the Sultan was the "Shadow of God" on earth and demanded absolute loyalty and submission from his nobles and subjects.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Which of the following sultans is known to abolish taxes on food?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **Sikandar Lodi**.

**Sikandar Lodi**, who ruled the **Lodi Dynasty**, introduced several administrative reforms to strengthen his economy and provide relief to his subjects. He is specifically remembered for abolishing the **zakat** (tax) on food grains, which made essential food items more affordable for the common people.

He also implemented a uniform system of land measurement known as the **Gaj-i-Sikandari**, which helped in standardizing agricultural taxation and preventing exploitation by local officials.

* **Iltutmish** is known for establishing the **Iqta system**.
* **Ibrahim Lodi** was the last ruler of the **Lodi Dynasty** and was defeated in the **First Battle of Panipat**.
* **Alauddin Khilji** is famous for his **market control regulations** and price fixing, rather than abolishing food taxes.

Related Facts:
* He shifted the capital from **Delhi** to **Agra** in 1504.
* He was a patron of learning and ordered the translation of Sanskrit medical texts into Persian.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Which of the following did not contribute to the construction of Qutub Minar
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **Alauddin Khilji**.

The construction of the **Qutub Minar** was a collaborative effort spanning several centuries and different rulers:

1. **Qutbuddin Aibak**: He started the construction of the tower in 1193 AD, completing only the first story.

2. **Iltutmish**: As the successor of Aibak, he added three more stories to the structure, bringing it to a total of four levels.

3. **Ferozeshah Tughlaq**: After a lightning strike damaged the top story in the 14^(th) century, he repaired it and added a fifth story to the monument.

**Alauddin Khilji**, while a prominent Sultan of the **Delhi Sultanate**, did not participate in the building of the Qutub Minar. Instead, he is famous for constructing the **Alai Darwaza**, which serves as the grand southern gateway to the Qutub complex.

It is a common point of confusion because both rulers were active in the same architectural complex, but their projects were distinct.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Who laid the foundation of the Mamluk dynasty?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The foundation of the **Mamluk dynasty** (also known as the **Slave dynasty**) was laid by **Qutbuddin Aibak** in 1206 CE.

He was a trusted general of **Muhammad Ghori**. Following the death of Ghori, Aibak established his independent rule in **Delhi**, marking the beginning of the **Delhi Sultanate**.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

* **Ala-ud-din** refers to Ala-ud-din Khalji, who belonged to the **Khalji dynasty**, the second dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate.
* **Ibrahim Lodi** was the last ruler of the **Lodi dynasty**, which was the final dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate before the Mughal Empire began.
* **Diwan-i-Amir kohi** is not a person; it was a **department of agriculture** created by **Muhammad bin Tughlaq** to promote farming.

**Qutbuddin Aibak** is also famously known for starting the construction of the **Qutub Minar** in Delhi. He earned the title **Lakh Baksh** (giver of lakhs) due to his immense generosity.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Qutb-ud-din shifted his capital to Delhi from which place?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **Lahore**.

**Qutb-ud-din Aibak**, the founder of the **Slave Dynasty** (or Mamluk Dynasty), initially governed his territories from **Lahore**.

When he established the **Delhi Sultanate** in 1206 AD, he continued to operate from Lahore due to its strategic importance in protecting his borders against rivals in Central Asia.

His successor, **Iltutmish**, is the one who officially shifted the capital from Lahore to **Delhi**. Delhi became the permanent administrative center and the seat of power for the Sultanate under his reign.

Regarding the other options:
* **Daulatabad** was famously made the capital later by **Muhammad bin Tughlaq** in his attempt to move the center of his empire.
* **Agra** was later developed as a capital by the **Lodi dynasty** and the **Mughals**, particularly under **Sikandar Lodi** and **Akbar**.
* **Pune** served as the seat of power for the **Marathas** much later in history.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Who laid the foundation of the city Tughlaqabad near Delhi?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **Ghiyas-ud-din Tughluq**.

**Ghiyas-ud-din Tughluq**, the founder of the **Tughlaq Dynasty**, established the city of **Tughlaqabad** in **1321 AD**. He built this city as his new capital, characterized by its massive, imposing stone fortifications and a distinct sloping wall design.

The city is famous for the **Tughlaqabad Fort**, which served as a defensive stronghold. It was designed to protect the sultanate from potential Mongol invasions.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

* **Ibrahim Lodi** was the last ruler of the Lodi dynasty and did not build Tughlaqabad.
* **Iltutmish** was a prominent ruler of the Slave Dynasty who ruled long before the Tughlaq dynasty existed.
* **Firoz Shah Tughlaq** was a later ruler of the Tughlaq dynasty; while he was a prolific builder of cities like Firozabad and Hisar, he did not found Tughlaqabad.

Legend suggests that the city was eventually abandoned due to a curse from the Sufi saint **Nizamuddin Auliya**, after the Sultan demanded the laborers stop working on the saint's water tank to work on the fort instead.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Who patronised the famous persian poet Amir Khusru?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The famous Persian poet **Amir Khusru** was primarily patronized by **Ghiyas ud-Din Balban**, the ninth Sultan of the **Mamluk dynasty** of Delhi. He joined Balban's court at a young age and later served under several subsequent rulers, earning him the title of the "Parrot of India" (*Tuti-e-Hind*).

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

* **Amir Khusru** is the name of the poet himself, not a patron.
* **Iltutmish** was an earlier ruler of the Mamluk dynasty and preceded the era where Amir Khusru became a prominent court poet.
* **Ibrahim Lodi** was the final ruler of the Lodi dynasty, which ended long after the era of the early Delhi Sultanate poets.

**Amir Khusru** is celebrated for his immense contribution to **Indo-Persian culture**. He is often credited with the invention of the **Sitar** and the creation of the **Qawwali** musical tradition in India.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Who was the successor of Muhammad-bin Tughlaq?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct successor of **Muhammad-bin Tughlaq** was **Firoz Shah Tughlaq**. He ascended the throne in **1351 AD** following the sudden death of Muhammad-bin Tughlaq at Thatta.

Here is the breakdown of why the other options are incorrect:

*   **Firoz Shah Tughlaq** was the cousin of Muhammad-bin Tughlaq and was chosen by the nobles and the army to restore stability to the empire.
*   **Ghiyas-ud-din Tughluq** was the founder of the **Tughlaq Dynasty** and the father of Muhammad-bin Tughlaq, reigning before him.
*   **Qutbuddin Aibak** was the founder of the **Slave Dynasty** (Mamluk Dynasty), reigning much earlier in the 13^(th) century.
*   **Ala-ud-din** (Khalji) belonged to the **Khalji Dynasty**, which preceded the Tughlaq rule entirely.

**Firoz Shah Tughlaq** is best remembered for his public welfare projects, such as building canals, hospitals, and educational institutions, as well as his extensive **irrigation works**. He also founded cities like **Hisar**, **Firozpur**, and **Jaunpur**.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: What was the language of administration under the Delhi Sultans?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct language of administration under the **Delhi Sultans** was **Persian**.

While the declared option suggests Urdu, that is historically inaccurate for the period of the Delhi Sultanate. Urdu emerged much later as a synthesis of various languages in military camps and market towns, whereas **Persian** was the official language of the court, literature, and administration.

Here is why **Persian** is the correct choice:

*   **Persian influence:** The Sultans were influenced by Persian culture and statecraft, leading them to adopt it as the language of record-keeping and official decrees.
*   **Literary tradition:** Most court historians, such as **Barani** and **Minhaj-i-Siraj**, wrote their chronicles in **Persian**.
*   **Administrative efficiency:** It served as a common medium for the ruling class, who were largely of Turkic or Afghan origin, to govern a diverse population.

**English** was not introduced as an administrative language until the period of British colonial rule in India. **Sanskrit** remained the language of religious and scholarly Hindu texts, but it was not used for the day-to-day governance of the Sultanate. **Urdu** only began to develop its distinct identity during the later Mughal period and did not hold official status under the Delhi Sultans.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Tarikh or Tawarikh were written in __________
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **Persian**.

**Tarikh** (plural: **Tawarikh**) refers to the valuable chronicles or historical records written by scholars, administrators, and courtiers during the **Delhi Sultanate** and **Mughal Empire** periods in India.

Here is why **Persian** is the accurate choice:

*   **Official Language:** **Persian** was the administrative and literary language of the Delhi Sultans and the Mughals.
*   **Literary Tradition:** Most historians of this era, such as **Ziauddin Barani** and **Minhaj-i-Siraj**, composed their works in **Persian** to document the reigns of various rulers.
*   **Cultural Influence:** These chronicles provide critical insights into the political, social, and cultural conditions of medieval India, serving as primary sources for modern historians.

While the declared answer mentioned Urdu, it is important to note that **Urdu** evolved much later as a distinct language through the interaction of Persian, Arabic, and local dialects. In the context of medieval historical records, **Persian** remains the primary language of authorship for these texts. **Sanskrit** was the language of classical Hindu literature, and **English** only became influential during the colonial period.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Raziyya Sultan ruled from __________ to 1240 AD
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
**Raziyya Sultan**, the daughter of **Iltutmish**, was the first and only female ruler of the **Delhi Sultanate**. She ascended the throne after the brief and ineffective reign of her brother, **Rukn-ud-din Firuz**.

Her reign began in **1236 AD**. She successfully took control of the administration and proved to be an efficient and bold leader, despite facing stiff opposition from the powerful Turkish nobles known as the **Chahalgani**.

She ruled for approximately four years, from **1236 to 1240 AD**. Her rule ended tragically due to a conspiracy by the disgruntled nobility, leading to her death near Kaithal in 1240 AD.

Therefore, **1236** is the correct starting date for her rule. Options 1233, 1239, and 1222 do not mark the beginning of her tenure as the Sultan of Delhi.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Delhi’s authority was challenged by __________ invasions
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **Mongols**.

During the **Delhi Sultanate** period, particularly under the reign of the **Khilji** and **Tughlaq** dynasties, the northwestern frontiers of India faced severe and recurring threats from the **Mongols**.

These invasions were a major concern for rulers like **Alauddin Khilji** and **Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq**. To counter this, they were forced to maintain a **large standing army** and implement strict military reforms, such as the **Dagh** (branding of horses) and **Chehra** (descriptive roll of soldiers) systems.

Here is why the other options do not fit the historical context of challenging the Delhi Sultanate's authority:

* **Marathas**: Their rise to prominence occurred much later, primarily challenging the declining **Mughal Empire** in the 17th and 18th centuries.
* **Mughals**: The Mughals were the successors who eventually established their own empire in India, defeating the last of the Delhi Sultans (the Lodi dynasty) at the **First Battle of Panipat** in 1526, rather than challenging the Sultanate from the outside as a periodic invading force.

The Mongol threat was persistent throughout the 13th and 14th centuries, shaping the defensive policies and administrative structure of the early Delhi rulers.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Who built Quwwat Ul Islam?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **Qutbuddin Aibak**.

**Quwwat-ul-Islam** (meaning "Might of Islam") is widely recognized as the first mosque built by the **Delhi Sultanate**. It is located within the **Qutub Minar** complex in Delhi.

**Qutbuddin Aibak**, the founder of the **Slave Dynasty** (or Mamluk Dynasty), commissioned the construction of this mosque in 1193 AD. It was built using the spoils of 27 demolished Hindu and Jain temples.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

* **Ibrahim Lodi** was the last ruler of the **Lodi Dynasty** and was defeated by Babur at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526.
* **Alauddin Khilji** was a powerful ruler of the **Khilji Dynasty** who significantly expanded the mosque complex, including the construction of the **Alai Darwaza**, but he did not build the original mosque.
* **Sikandar Lodi** was a Lodi ruler known for shifting his capital to Agra and did not construct the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque.

An interesting historical fact is that the **Qutub Minar** minaret was also initiated by **Qutbuddin Aibak** to serve as a tower for the muezzin to call the faithful to prayer at this very mosque.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Balban was a Sultan of which dynasty?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
**Ghiyas-ud-din Balban** was a prominent ruler belonging to the **Slave Dynasty**, also known as the **Mamluk Dynasty** or the **Ilbari Dynasty**.

The correct option is **3**. Although the provided list suggests a different answer, historical records confirm that Balban served as the ninth Sultan of the **Slave Dynasty** in the **Delhi Sultanate**.

Here is a quick breakdown to clarify:

*   **Slave Dynasty (1206–1290):** This was the first dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate, established by Qutb-ud-din Aibak. Balban was the most powerful ruler of this lineage, reigning from 1266 to 1287.
*   **The Khilji Dynasty:** This dynasty succeeded the Slave Dynasty, founded by Jalal-ud-din Khilji after the decline of Balban's successors.
*   **The Lodi Dynasty:** This was the final dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate, coming much later in history (1451–1526).
*   **The Sayyad Dynasty:** This dynasty ruled between the Tughlaq and Lodi periods.

Balban is best remembered for his **Theory of Kingship**, where he declared that the Sultan was the "Shadow of God" on earth. He also introduced the Persian customs of **Sijda** (prostration) and **Paibos** (kissing the monarch's feet) to maintain the dignity of the throne.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: First battle of Tarain held in which year?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The **First Battle of Tarain** took place in **1191 AD**.

This historic conflict was fought between the **Chahamana (Chauhan) King Prithviraj Chauhan** and the **Ghurid ruler Muhammad Ghori**.

The battle occurred near the town of **Tarain** (modern-day Taraori in Haryana, India).

Key points to remember:

*   **Outcome:** Prithviraj Chauhan emerged victorious in this battle, successfully repelling the initial Ghurid invasion.
*   **Muhammad Ghori:** Despite his defeat in 1191, Ghori regrouped and returned the following year.
*   **Second Battle of Tarain:** This follow-up battle occurred in **1192 AD**, where Muhammad Ghori defeated Prithviraj Chauhan, marking a turning point for Islamic rule in India.

The other options are incorrect because they do not correspond to the dates of these specific historical encounters. Remembering the sequence of 1191 and 1192 is crucial for TNPSC history questions.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Muslim Rule in India was established by whom?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **Muhammad Ghori**.

While the options provided suggest otherwise, historical evidence confirms that **Muhammad Ghori** is the true architect of Muslim rule in India. His victory in the **Second Battle of Tarain** in 1192 CE against Prithviraj Chauhan laid the foundation for long-term Islamic governance in the region.

Here is the breakdown of why the other figures do not fit this specific historical milestone:

*   **Muhammad Ghori**: He shifted the focus from mere plundering raids to the establishment of an empire. After his victory, he appointed his general, **Qutbuddin Aibak**, to manage the captured territories, effectively launching the **Delhi Sultanate**.

*   **Qutbuddin Aibak**: As the commander of Ghori's forces, he became the first independent ruler of the **Mamluk (Slave) Dynasty** in 1206 CE. While he consolidated the rule, the initial establishment was Ghori's achievement.

*   **Iltutmish**: Often considered the *real* consolidator of the Delhi Sultanate, he stabilized the empire established by his predecessor, Aibak. He was the third ruler, not the founder of the rule itself.

*   **Ibrahim Lodi**: He was the final ruler of the **Lodi Dynasty** and the Delhi Sultanate. His defeat at the **First Battle of Panipat** in 1526 CE by Babur actually marked the end of the Delhi Sultanate and the beginning of the **Mughal Empire**.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: In which century Muslim rule was established in India?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The establishment of Muslim rule in India is historically attributed to the conquests of **Muhammad Ghori** at the end of the **12th century**.

While there were earlier incursions, such as the Arab conquest of Sindh in the 8th century or the raids by **Mahmud of Ghazni** in the 11th century, these did not lead to permanent political consolidation.

The decisive shift occurred after the **Second Battle of Tarain** in **1192 AD**.

Following this victory, Muhammad Ghori and his general, **Qutb-ud-din Aibak**, laid the foundation for the **Delhi Sultanate**.

Consequently, the **12th century** serves as the period when the administrative structure of Muslim rule began to take root in Northern India, eventually leading to the formal establishment of the **Slave Dynasty** in the early **13th century**.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: What was the period of the Mamluk Dynasty?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **1206-1290**.

The **Mamluk Dynasty**, also known as the **Slave Dynasty**, was the first dynasty of the **Delhi Sultanate**. It was founded by **Qutb ud-Din Aibak** in 1206 following the death of **Muhammad Ghori**.

This dynasty ruled northern India for nearly 84 years, establishing the foundations of Islamic rule in the region. The period ended in 1290 when **Jalal ud-Din Firuz Khalji** overthrew the last Mamluk ruler, **Muiz ud-Din Qaiqabad**, marking the beginning of the **Khalji Dynasty**.

* The other options represent different timelines that do not align with the historical transition from the Slave dynasty to the Khalji dynasty.

Related Facts:
* The term **Mamluk** refers to a soldier of slave origin who converted to Islam.
* **Iltutmish** and **Razia Sultana** were among the most prominent rulers of this dynasty.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: What was the period of the Tughlaq Dynasty?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The **Tughlaq Dynasty** ruled over the **Delhi Sultanate** from **1320 AD** to **1414 AD**.

They succeeded the **Khalji Dynasty** and were followed by the **Sayyid Dynasty**. The founder of the dynasty was **Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq**, who rose to power after the death of the last Khalji ruler.

The Tughlaq period is historically significant for being the most extensive phase of the Delhi Sultanate in terms of geographical reach, particularly during the reign of **Muhammad bin Tughlaq**.

The dynasty eventually declined following the devastating invasion of **Timur** in 1398 AD, which weakened their central authority significantly. By 1414 AD, **Khizr Khan**, the governor of Multan, took control of Delhi and established the Sayyid Dynasty.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: What was the period of the Sayyid Dynasty?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The **Sayyid Dynasty** ruled the **Delhi Sultanate** between **1414** and **1451**.

The correct option is **1414-1451**.

Here is a quick breakdown of why this is the correct timeframe:

*   The dynasty was founded by **Khizr Khan** in **1414** after he took control of Delhi following the decline of the Tughlaq dynasty.
*   The rule ended in **1451** when the last ruler, **Ala-ud-din Alam Shah**, abdicated the throne.
*   **Bahlul Lodi**, the governor of Lahore, subsequently took over power and established the **Lodi Dynasty**.

To help you remember, here is the chronological order of the Delhi Sultanate dynasties:
1. **Slave Dynasty** (1206-1290)
2. **Khilji Dynasty** (1290-1320)
3. **Tughlaq Dynasty** (1320-1414)
4. **Sayyid Dynasty** (1414-1451)
5. **Lodi Dynasty** (1451-1526)

Option 3 (1206-1290) actually refers to the **Slave Dynasty**, also known as the **Mamluk Dynasty**, established by **Qutb-ud-din Aibak**.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Which one of the following is written by Ibn Battuta?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **Rehla**.

**Ibn Battuta**, a famous Moroccan scholar and traveler, visited India during the reign of **Muhammad bin Tughlaq**. His travelogue, titled **Rihla** (or **The Travels**), provides detailed and valuable historical information about the 14th-century social, political, and cultural life in the Delhi Sultanate.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

*   **Arthashastra**: This foundational treatise on statecraft, economic policy, and military strategy was written by **Chanakya** (also known as Kautilya) during the Maurya Empire.
*   **Dihal**: This term does not correspond to a major historical work associated with Ibn Battuta or other prominent travelers in the context of Indian history.
*   **Discovery of India**: This influential book was written by **Jawaharlal Nehru** during his imprisonment in the Ahmednagar Fort in the 1940s, long after the medieval period.

**Ibn Battuta's** account is specifically noted by historians for its vivid descriptions of the postal system, the court of the Sultan, and the diverse customs of the people he encountered across his extensive journeys.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Which of the following books was written by Al-Biruni?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **Kitab-ul Hind**.

**Al-Biruni**, a renowned scholar and polymath from the 11th century, authored this monumental work during his travels to India. His writing provides an exhaustive and objective account of Indian culture, science, philosophy, and religion during that era.

Regarding the other options:
* **Rehla** is the famous travelogue written by the explorer **Ibn Battuta**.
* **Arthashastra** is the ancient Indian political treatise composed by **Chanakya**.
* **Dihal** is not a historical text associated with Al-Biruni.

Related Facts:
* **Al-Biruni** is often referred to as the founder of Indology.
* The full title of his book is **Kitab fi Tahqiq ma li-l-Hind**.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Who among the following belonged to Morocco?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **Ibn Battuta**.

**Ibn Battuta** was a famous medieval scholar and explorer born in **Tangier, Morocco**, in 1304. He is renowned for his extensive travels across the Islamic world, covering over 75,000 miles throughout Africa, Asia, and Europe.

He visited India during the reign of **Muhammad bin Tughlaq** and served as a *Qazi* (judge) in the Delhi Sultanate for several years. His experiences and observations are detailed in his famous travelogue, the **Rihla**.

Regarding the other options:

* **Fahien** was a Chinese Buddhist monk who visited India during the reign of **Chandragupta II** (Gupta dynasty) to collect Buddhist scriptures.
* **Al-Biruni** was a Persian scholar from modern-day **Uzbekistan** who accompanied **Mahmud of Ghazni** to India and wrote the famous work **Kitab-ul-Hind**.

Since Ibn Battuta is the only traveler from Morocco, the first option is the correct choice.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Who belongs to Uzbekistan?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **Al-Biruni**.

**Al-Biruni** was a legendary polymath born in **Khwarezm**, a region that is located in modern-day **Uzbekistan**. He is widely recognized for his profound contributions to **astronomy**, **mathematics**, **geography**, and **history**.

He accompanied **Mahmud of Ghazni** to India and authored the famous book ***Kitab-ul-Hind***, which provides an extensive account of Indian culture and science during the 11th century.

Here is why the other options are excluded:

* **Ibn Battuta** was a famous traveler and scholar from **Morocco**, known for his extensive travels across the Islamic world and beyond.

* **Fahien** (Faxian) was a **Chinese** Buddhist monk who traveled to India during the reign of the Gupta emperor **Chandragupta II** to collect Buddhist scriptures.

Since **Al-Biruni** is the only figure associated with the geographical region of Uzbekistan, he is the correct choice.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: What was the period of Khilji Dynasty?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The **Khilji Dynasty** was the second dynasty of the **Delhi Sultanate**. It held power in Northern India for exactly 30 years.

The dynasty was founded by **Jalal-ud-din Firuz Khilji** in **1290 AD**, after he overthrew the Mamluk dynasty.

The reign of the Khiljis ended in **1320 AD** when **Ghiyath al-Din Tughluq** defeated the last ruler, Khusrau Khan, and established the **Tughluq Dynasty**.

Therefore, the correct chronological period is **1290-1320**.

This period is particularly famous for the reign of **Alauddin Khilji**, who expanded the Sultanate deep into Southern India and implemented significant market reforms and military innovations.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: During whose period several Sanskrit books dealing with mathematics,medicine and yoga were translated into Persian?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **Sikandar Lodi**.

During the reign of **Sikandar Lodi** (1489–1517 AD), there was a significant cultural exchange between the Persian-speaking administration and the Indian traditions.

Here is why this development is historically significant:

*   **Sikandar Lodi** was a patron of learning and literature. He actively encouraged the translation of **Sanskrit** works into **Persian**.
*   A notable achievement of his period was the translation of a famous Sanskrit work on **Ayurveda** (Indian medicine), which was titled **Tibb-i-Sikandari**.
*   This process helped bridge the gap between Islamic scholarship and ancient Indian sciences like **mathematics**, **yoga**, and **medicine**.

The other options are incorrect because:

*   **Alam Shah** was the last ruler of the Sayyid dynasty and did not preside over a major cultural synthesis of this nature.
*   **Muhammad Ghori** was primarily focused on military expansion and the establishment of Turkish rule in India rather than literary translation projects.
*   **Bahlol Lodi**, while the founder of the Lodi dynasty, spent most of his reign consolidating power and managing tribal politics among the Afghans.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Who is called as Prime minister in the Sultanate period?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **Wazir**.

During the **Delhi Sultanate**, the central administration was headed by the **Sultan**, but the **Wazir** served as his chief minister or Prime Minister.

The office of the Wazir was known as the **Wizarat**. Their primary responsibility was to oversee the **Diwan-i-Wizarat**, which managed the state's financial administration and revenue collection.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

* **Diwan-i-Arz**: This department was in charge of military affairs. The head of this office was called the **Ariz-i-Mumalik**.

* **Diwan-i-Amir Kohi**: Established by Muhammad bin Tughlaq, this department focused exclusively on **agriculture** and state-sponsored farming projects.

* **Diwan-i-Insha**: This department handled royal correspondence and managed the drafting of official documents and proclamations issued by the Sultan.

In essence, while other officials managed specific sectors like defense or agriculture, the **Wazir** held the highest position of authority under the Sultan, coordinating the overall governance of the empire.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: In which year Alauddin Khilji invaded Devagiri?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
**Alauddin Khilji** invaded **Devagiri** in the year **1296** AD.

At the time of this invasion, **Alauddin Khilji** was the governor of **Kara-Manikpur** and served under his uncle, the Sultan **Jalaluddin Khilji**. This campaign was a clandestine expedition launched without the Sultan's explicit permission.

The target of his attack was the **Yadava** ruler, **Ramachandra Deva**. Alauddin's success in this mission brought him immense wealth, including gold, silver, and precious stones, which he subsequently used to consolidate his power and eventually usurp the throne of Delhi.

Here is why the other options do not fit:

* **1292**: This year is generally associated with earlier military expeditions, such as the invasion of Bhilsa.
* **1299**: This year marks the invasion of **Gujarat**, another significant military campaign led by Alauddin's generals, Ulugh Khan and Nusrat Khan.
* **1293**: This period does not represent the primary date for the historical conquest of the Yadava kingdom.

The success at **Devagiri** is considered a pivotal moment in the history of the **Khilji Dynasty**, as it provided the financial resources necessary to strengthen the military and expand the empire southward.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Who translated the Greek work of Euclid into Sanskrit?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **Alberuni**.

**Alberuni** (also known as Abu Rayhan al-Biruni) was a profound scholar and polymath who accompanied Mahmud of Ghazni to India. During his extensive studies of Indian culture, science, and philosophy, he translated several Greek works into Sanskrit to facilitate the exchange of knowledge between the two traditions.

His most notable achievement in this area was translating **Euclid's Elements** and **Ptolemy's Almagest** into Sanskrit. This effort was aimed at introducing Hellenistic mathematical and astronomical concepts to the scholarly community in India.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

* **Iltutmish** and **Balban** were rulers of the **Slave Dynasty** (Delhi Sultanate). While they were significant political figures, their reigns were primarily focused on consolidating power and administration rather than academic translation work.
* **Amir Khusro** was a legendary poet, musician, and scholar in the court of various Delhi Sultans. Although he was a prolific writer known as the "Parrot of India," he is not credited with translating the works of Euclid.

**Alberuni** is frequently cited in TNPSC exams for his monumental work, **Kitab-ul-Hind**, which provides an objective and detailed account of Indian society, science, and religion during the 11th century.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Who emerged as a major figure of Persian prose and poetry?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **Amir Khusro**.

**Amir Khusro** is widely recognized as a legendary figure in the history of **Persian literature** in India. He was a prolific poet and writer who served under several **Delhi Sultanate** rulers.

He is famously known as the **"Parrot of India"** (*Tuti-e-Hind*) due to his mastery of the Persian language and his significant contributions to both Persian and **Hindustani** poetry.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

* **Alberuni** was a brilliant scholar and polymath who wrote *Kitab-ul-Hind*. While he was a master of Persian and Arabic, his primary contributions were in **history, geography, and science** rather than being defined primarily as a figure of Persian creative prose and poetry in the same literary sense as Khusro.
* **Balban** was a powerful **Sultan of Delhi** known for his administrative and military reforms, such as the policy of **Blood and Iron**. He was a patron of literature, not a literary figure himself.

**Amir Khusro's** influence was so profound that he is also credited with the creation of several musical forms and the synthesis of **Persian, Arabic, and Indian musical traditions**.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Who proclaimed that Indian music had a preeminence over all the other music of the world?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **Amir Khusro**.

**Amir Khusro**, often celebrated as the **"Parrot of India"** (*Tuti-e-Hind*), was a prolific poet, musician, and scholar who lived during the Sultanate period. He held a deep appreciation for the musical traditions of India.

In his historical works, specifically within the **Nuh Sipihr** (The Nine Heavens), he famously proclaimed the superiority of Indian music. He argued that Indian music possessed a unique power to captivate the human soul and even influence animals, granting it a **preeminence** over all other musical systems known at that time.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

*   **Sikandar Lodi** was a ruler of the Lodi dynasty known for his administrative reforms and religious policies, but he is not recognized for scholarly treatises on the aesthetics of music.
*   **Iltutmish** was a prominent ruler of the Mamluk dynasty, primarily focused on consolidating the Delhi Sultanate and managing political threats rather than musical theory.
*   **Ibrahim Lodi** was the final ruler of the Lodi dynasty, whose reign was defined by military conflict and political instability, leaving no scholarly contribution to musicology.

**Amir Khusro** is also credited with synthesizing Persian and Indian musical traditions, which led to the evolution of **Qawwali** and the development of classical instruments like the **Sitar** and **Tabla**. His work remains a bridge between the Islamic traditions of Central Asia and the indigenous classical music of the Indian subcontinent.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi contains the history of which dynasty?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The **Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi** is a historical work primarily associated with the **Tughlaq Dynasty**. It was authored by **Ziauddin Barani** during the reign of **Firoz Shah Tughlaq**.

The book covers the history of the **Delhi Sultanate** starting from the reign of **Ghiyas-ud-din Balban** of the Slave Dynasty up to the early years of the reign of **Firoz Shah Tughlaq**. Because it provides extensive details regarding the administrative and political history of the **Tughlaq** rulers, it is categorized under the history of the **Tughlaq Dynasty**.

*   **Ziauddin Barani** serves as the primary source for the Sultanate period.
*   The text is highly valued by historians for its insights into the socio-economic conditions and governance under the **Tughlaqs**.
*   While the work touches upon previous dynasties, its focus and dedication to the era of **Firoz Shah** align it most closely with the **Tughlaq** period.

The other options, such as the **Lodi**, **Sayyid**, and **Khilji** dynasties, are covered by different chroniclers or distinct historical accounts rather than being the central focus of Barani's work.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Who effectively repulsed the Mongol army that had marched up to Meerut near Delhi?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **Muhammad Tughlaq** (Muhammad bin Tughlaq).

During the reign of the **Tughlaq dynasty**, the **Chagatai Khanate** Mongols, led by **Tarmashirin**, launched a massive invasion into India. They advanced deep into the subcontinent, reaching as far as **Meerut**, located near the capital, **Delhi**.

**Muhammad bin Tughlaq** demonstrated remarkable military strategy during this crisis. He managed to force the Mongols to retreat, either through a decisive military engagement or by paying a massive ransom to induce their withdrawal.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

* **Sikandar Lodi** and **Ibrahim Lodi** belonged to the later **Lodi dynasty**, which ruled long after the primary Mongol threat to the Delhi Sultanate had subsided.
* **Muhammad Ghori** lived in the 12th century, long before the Mongol Empire expanded into the Indian frontier during the 13th and 14th centuries.

This event is a significant point in **Delhi Sultanate** history as it highlights the constant pressure the Sultans faced from the **Mongol threat** to the northwest. Following this invasion, the Tughlaq administration significantly fortified the northern defenses to prevent further incursions.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Muhammad bin tughlaq ascended the throne in which year?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **1325**.

**Muhammad bin Tughlaq** ascended the throne of the **Delhi Sultanate** following the death of his father, **Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq**.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:
* **1321** marks the beginning of the Tughlaq dynasty under Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq, not the start of Muhammad bin Tughlaq's reign.
* **1322** and **1324** fall within the reign of his father, who ruled from 1321 to 1325.

Muhammad bin Tughlaq is historically noted for his ambitious but controversial administrative experiments, such as shifting the capital from **Delhi to Daulatabad** and the introduction of **token currency**. He was a highly educated ruler known for his interest in philosophy, medicine, and mathematics, yet he faced numerous rebellions throughout his long reign ending in 1351.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Tomaras rules which region?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The **Tomara dynasty** ruled over the region of **Delhi** and parts of Haryana during the early medieval period.

They were a prominent Rajput clan who established their capital at **Dhillika**, which is known today as Delhi.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:
* **Mumbai** was historically ruled by various powers like the Silharas and later the Portuguese and British, not the Tomaras.
* **Pune** was a significant center under the Yadavas of Devagiri and later became the seat of the Peshwas during the Maratha Empire.
* **Agra** gained major historical prominence much later under the Lodi dynasty and the Mughal Empire.

**Historical context:**
The Tomaras are credited with founding the city of Delhi in the 8th century. They were later succeeded by the **Chauhan** (Chahamana) dynasty, most notably under the rule of **Prithviraj Chauhan**.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Chaugans are ruled in which region?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **Rajasthan**. The **Chauhans** (also known as **Chahamanas**) primarily established their rule in the **Ajmer** and **Sambhar** regions, which are located in modern-day **Rajasthan**. They were a prominent Rajput clan who played a significant role in the history of North India.

Their power reached its peak under famous rulers like **Prithviraj Chauhan**, who expanded their influence significantly. While they also exerted authority over parts of Delhi and Haryana later on, their heartland and historical origins remain firmly rooted in Rajasthan.

Other options are incorrect because:
* **Delhi** was a major city they contested, but it was not their original base or region of primary control.
* **Mumbai** and **Pune** are located in the Maharashtra region and were not under the rule of the Chauhan dynasty.

Related Facts:
* The Chahamanas were originally feudatories of the **Gurjara-Pratiharas**.
* The legendary **Ajayameru** (Ajmer) was founded by the Chauhan king **Ajayaraja II**.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Bernier's Books were published in france in the year of __________
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **1670-1671**.

**François Bernier**, a French physician and traveler, documented his experiences in the Mughal Empire during the reign of **Aurangzeb**. These historical accounts provided Europeans with a detailed understanding of Indian society, economy, and politics during the 17th century.

His primary work, titled *Travels in the Mogul Empire*, was first published in **Paris** in the years **1670-1671**. This text remains a vital primary source for scholars studying the administrative and social structure of the Mughal era.

Other options are incorrect because they fall outside the specific timeframe in which Bernier prepared and published his journals regarding his travels in the East.

Related Facts:
* Bernier lived in India for about 12 years from 1656 to 1668.
* He served as a physician to Prince Dara Shikoh, the eldest son of Shah Jahan.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: The European traveller who visited India and China is?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **Marco Polo**.

**Marco Polo** was a famous Venetian merchant and explorer who traveled extensively across Asia in the 13th century. His journey took him along the **Silk Road**, allowing him to visit both **India** and the court of **Kublai Khan** in **China**.

Here is why the other options do not fit this specific description:

* **Ibn Battuta** was a Moroccan scholar known for his massive travels across the Islamic world, including India and China, but he is categorized as a traveler from the Islamic world rather than a "European" in the traditional historical sense used for this question.
* **Francois Bernier** was a French physician and traveler who spent several years in the Mughal court of **Aurangzeb** in India during the 17th century, but he did not travel to China.
* **Al-Biruni** was a Persian scholar who arrived in India alongside **Mahmud of Ghazni** in the 11th century; he is famous for his work *Kitab-ul-Hind*, but he was not a European traveler.

**Marco Polo's** detailed accounts of his travels were recorded in his book, *The Travels of Marco Polo*. His descriptions of the wealth and culture of the East profoundly influenced European cartography and the Age of Discovery.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: In which century Important descriptions of Vijayanagar were given?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **15th century**.

During the **15th century**, several prominent foreign travelers visited the **Vijayanagara Empire**. These travelers provided detailed written accounts of the city's administration, architecture, and the daily lives of its people, which remain vital historical records for us today.

Notable visitors like **Nicolo de Conti** (an Italian) and **Abdur Razzaq** (a Persian diplomat) came to the capital city of **Hampi** during this century. Their observations give us an excellent picture of the empire's prosperity.

The other options are incorrect because the empire was only founded in **1336 AD** (14th century). While travelers continued to arrive in the **16th century**, the most foundational and comprehensive descriptions of the city's peak during its earlier development come from the mid-15th century accounts.

Related Facts:
* **Nicolo de Conti** visited Vijayanagara around 1420 AD.
* **Abdur Razzaq** visited the court of Deva Raya II in 1443 AD.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Tarabad means?
options: Marketplace for male and Female singers
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **Marketplace for male and Female singers**.

In the context of historical Indian markets, the term **Tarabad** specifically refers to a designated space or marketplace where professional singers, dancers, and performers gathered to practice their art and trade their services.

* Other options are incorrect because **Tarabad** was not a general public market or a marketplace exclusively for the king, but rather a hub specifically associated with the performing arts community.

Related Facts:
* These markets were often found in major medieval cities where the performing arts were highly patronized by the nobility.
* They served as both a place for performance and a residential area for artists.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Who founded Delhi as a city full of exciting opportunities?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **Ibn Battuta**.

**Ibn Battuta**, the famous Moroccan traveler, arrived in India during the reign of **Muhammad bin Tughlaq** in the 14th century. In his travelogue, the **Rihla**, he vividly described **Delhi** as a vast, magnificent city with a dense population and immense wealth.

He specifically characterized Delhi as a city of **exciting opportunities**, noting that it served as a major center for scholars, merchants, and adventurers from across the Islamic world. His account highlights the city's prosperity, administrative organization, and the vibrant social life maintained by the Sultanate.

To understand why the other options do not fit:

*   **Francois Bernier** was a French physician who visited India much later, during the **Mughal** era under Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb, primarily documenting the nature of land ownership.
*   **Al-Biruni** was a Persian scholar who arrived in India centuries before Ibn Battuta, during the time of Mahmud of Ghazni, and is best known for his detailed study of Indian culture and science in the **Kitab-ul-Hind**.
*   **Marco Polo** was a Venetian explorer who traveled extensively through Asia and parts of coastal India, but his primary accounts focus on maritime trade routes and the southern kingdoms rather than the interior urban life of the Delhi Sultanate.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: How many Gates were there in Delhi?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The historical city of **Shahjahanabad**, which is now known as **Old Delhi**, was a walled city commissioned by the Mughal Emperor **Shah Jahan** in the 17th century.

To regulate trade and movement, the city was enclosed by a massive stone wall fortified with **28 gates**.

These gates served as entry and exit points for the city, connecting it to various parts of the empire and neighboring regions. Some of the most famous among these include:

*   **Delhi Gate**
*   **Ajmeri Gate**
*   **Kashmiri Gate**
*   **Lahori Gate**
*   **Turkman Gate**

While many of these structures were damaged or removed during the expansion and modernization of the city, their names remain etched in the local geography and history of Delhi today. The number **28** is historically recognized as the total count of these defensive portals during the peak of the Mughal era.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Who saw the Mughal Empire – its king was the king of beggars and barbarians?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **Francois Bernier**.

**Francois Bernier** was a French physician and traveler who spent twelve years in India during the reign of **Aurangzeb**. He arrived in 1656 and served at the Mughal court, documenting his observations in the work titled *Travels in the Mogul Empire*.

His critique of the empire was harsh because he was accustomed to European systems of private property. He famously described the Mughal state as one where the **king was the king of beggars and barbarians**, arguing that the lack of private land ownership led to the impoverishment of the peasantry and the decay of the empire.

Other options can be eliminated based on their historical timelines:
* **Fahien**: A Chinese monk who visited India during the **Gupta period** (reign of Chandragupta II).
* **Ibn Battuta**: A Moroccan traveler who arrived in India during the **Delhi Sultanate** under the reign of Muhammad bin Tughlaq.
* **Al-Biruni**: A Persian scholar who arrived in India in the 11th century alongside **Mahmud of Ghazni**, long before the establishment of the Mughal Empire.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Mamluk means __________
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct meaning of the term **Mamluk** is **Slave**. Therefore, the third option is the historically accurate choice.

The word **Mamluk** originates from Arabic, specifically referring to a person who is owned or a **purchased slave**. In the context of medieval Islamic history, it specifically refers to soldiers of slave origin who eventually rose to positions of significant power.

The **Mamluk Sultanate** was a powerful empire that ruled over **Egypt** and **Syria** from 1250 to 1517. These rulers were originally soldiers brought from the Eurasian Steppe, particularly the **Turkic** and **Circassian** regions, who were trained in elite military tactics.

The other options provided, such as money, gold, or diamond, do not reflect the etymological or historical definition of the term. The Mamluks are famous for their military prowess, particularly their success in defeating the **Mongol Empire** at the **Battle of Ain Jalut** in 1260.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Who postulated that the shadow of the earth falling on the moon caused an eclipse?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **Aryabhatta**.

**Aryabhatta**, a renowned Indian mathematician and astronomer from the **Gupta period**, provided a scientific explanation for lunar and solar eclipses in his famous work, the ***Aryabhatiya***.

He moved away from the mythological beliefs of his time, which attributed eclipses to the demon Rahu. Instead, he mathematically proved that:

*   A **lunar eclipse** occurs when the **Earth** passes between the Sun and the Moon, casting its shadow on the lunar surface.
*   A **solar eclipse** is caused by the shadow of the **Moon** falling on the Earth.

His ability to calculate the size and distance of these celestial bodies with remarkable accuracy cemented his legacy as the father of Indian astronomy.

Regarding the other options:

*   **Varahamihira** was also a great astronomer who lived later and refined many of these concepts, but he credited the foundation of this specific observation to his predecessors.
*   **Panini** is best known as the father of **Sanskrit grammar** for his work, the *Ashtadhyayi*.
*   **Nagarjuna** was a celebrated **philosopher and chemist** known for his contributions to Mahayana Buddhism and the study of alchemy.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Kharaj means
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **Land tax from non-Muslims**.

**Kharaj** was a specific type of land tax levied on non-Muslim subjects, known as **dhimmis**, under Islamic rule. This tax was primarily collected from agricultural land and served as a key source of revenue for the state treasury during the period of the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughal Empire.

Other options are incorrect because:
* **Booty captured in the War** refers to **Khums**.
* **Religious tax on non-Muslims** refers to **Jizya**.
* **Land Tax from Muslim Peasants** refers to **Ushr**.

Related Facts:
* The collection of Kharaj was based on the productivity of the land.
* It represents the socio-economic structure of land revenue administration in medieval India.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Name the Historian who described Samudra Gupta as the Indian Napoleon?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct historian is **V.A. Smith**.

He famously described **Samudra Gupta** as the **Napoleon of India** in his renowned work, *Early History of India*.

**Why this title was given:**
*   **Military Genius:** Like Napoleon Bonaparte, Samudra Gupta was a brilliant military strategist who remained undefeated in battle.
*   **Vast Conquests:** He expanded the **Gupta Empire** significantly through his campaigns across Northern and Southern India, as detailed in the **Allahabad Pillar Inscription** (Prayag Prashasti) composed by his court poet, **Harisena**.

**Understanding the options:**
*   **V.A. Smith** is the author who coined this specific historical comparison.
*   **R.C. Majumdar** and **R.K. Mukherjee** were eminent historians of the Gupta period, but they are not credited with this specific titular analogy.
*   **H.C. Raychaudhuri** is well-known for his extensive research on the political history of ancient India, particularly his analysis of the rise of the **Magadha** kingdom.

**Key takeaway:**
The term serves to highlight Samudra Gupta's reputation as a **conqueror** and his immense role in political unification, though modern historians often suggest that the comparison is limited given the vast differences in the military contexts of their respective eras.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q:
Choose the wrong matches [Contemporaries of Alauddin Khilji]
1) Ramachandra Deva - Warrangal
2) Prataparudra Deva - Devagiri
3) Vira Ballala III - Dwarasamudra
4) Vira Pandiyan - Madurai
5) Ravi Varma - Kollam
6) Banu Deva - Orissa
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
To identify the incorrect matches, we must map the contemporary rulers to their respective kingdoms during the campaigns of **Alauddin Khilji** and his general **Malik Kafur**:

*   **Ramachandra Deva** was the ruler of the **Yadava** dynasty based in **Devagiri**, not Warrangal.
*   **Prataparudra Deva** was the ruler of the **Kakatiya** dynasty based in **Warrangal**, not Devagiri.

Because these two are swapped in the given list, statements (1) and (2) are both incorrect.

Regarding the other options:
*   **Vira Ballala III** of the **Hoysala** dynasty was indeed based in **Dwarasamudra**.
*   **Vira Pandiyan** was one of the claimants to the **Pandya** throne in **Madurai**.
*   **Ravi Varma** was the ruler of the **Chera** kingdom in **Kollam** (Quilon).
*   **Banu Deva** (Bhanudeva II) was the ruler of the **Eastern Ganga** dynasty in **Orissa**.

Since statements (3), (4), (5), and (6) accurately reflect the political landscape of the Deccan and South India during that era, only (1) and (2) contain factual errors regarding the kingdom-ruler association. Thus, option 1 is the correct choice.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: The Gupta emperors before Chandragupta-II issued only __________ coins
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **Gold**.

The Gupta coinage system is widely celebrated for its artistic beauty and purity. The gold coins issued by the early Gupta rulers were known as **Dinaras**.

Here is the step-by-step context for the early Gupta currency:

*   **Chandragupta I** was the first Gupta ruler to issue gold coins, which depicted the king and his queen, Kumara Devi.
*   **Samudragupta**, the successor of Chandragupta I, expanded the variety of these gold coins, featuring themes like the **Standard type**, **Archer type**, and the **Lyrist type**.
*   These emperors focused primarily on gold to demonstrate the immense wealth and economic stability of the **Gupta Empire**.

It was only later, under **Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya)**, that the empire began minting **Silver coins** on a large scale. This shift occurred after he conquered the Western Kshatrapas in Gujarat and Kathiawar, adopting their tradition of silver coinage to facilitate local trade.

Copper coins were minted by the Guptas as well, but they were significantly rarer and used primarily for smaller, everyday transactions. Therefore, the early gold standard remains the definitive hallmark of the pre-Chandragupta II era.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct option is **2**. **Ala-ud-din Khalji** reigned from **1296** to **1316**, making this the accurately matched pair.

Here is the breakdown of the historical timeline for the **Khalji Dynasty**:

* **Jalaluddin Firoz Khalji**: He founded the dynasty and ruled from **1290** to **1296**. Option 1 is incorrect because his reign began two years earlier than stated.

* **Ala-ud-din Khalji**: He succeeded Jalaluddin and ruled from **1296** to **1316**. This is the correct match. He is famous for his market reforms and for expanding the empire into Southern India.

* **Kutbudin Mubarak Shah**: He ruled from **1316** to **1320**. Option 3 is incorrect as the dates provided do not align with his actual tenure.

* **Nasiruddin Khusru Shah**: He ruled briefly in **1320**. Option 4 is incorrect, as he was the last ruler of the Khalji dynasty before the rise of the **Tughlaq Dynasty**.

Understanding these specific reign dates is essential for **TNPSC** exams, as they frequently test the chronological order of the **Delhi Sultanate** rulers. Always remember that the Khalji dynasty lasted only for thirty years, from **1290** to **1320**.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q:
Assertion [A] : Alaudin khilji imposed price control in Delhi
Reason [R] : He wanted to pay lower wages to artisans building his palaces in Delhi
options: Both [A] and [R] are true, and [R] is the correct explanation of [A]
Both [A] and [R] are true; but [R] is not the correct explanation of [A]
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
**Alauddin Khilji** did indeed introduce a comprehensive system of **price control** (market regulations) in Delhi. This was done to maintain a large standing army with limited financial resources, ensuring soldiers could live comfortably on fixed salaries despite the high cost of living.

The assertion [A] is therefore **true**.

However, the reason [R] claiming he imposed these controls specifically to pay lower wages to artisans is **false**. His market reforms were primarily driven by **military requirements** and the need to curb hoarding and black marketing, not by the desire to exploit palace artisans.

The correct option is **3** ([A] is true, but [R] is false).

Key points about his market reforms:
*   He established three distinct markets: one for **food grains**, one for **expensive cloths/sugar/dried fruits**, and one for **horses, slaves, and cattle**.
*   He appointed **Shahna-i-Mandi** (superintendent of markets) to monitor the supply and prices of goods.
*   He created a massive grain storage system in Delhi to prevent shortages during times of famine or drought.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Alam Shah was the Last Sultan of Sayyid Dynasty. What was the original name of Alam Shah?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The original name of **Alam Shah**, the last ruler of the **Sayyid Dynasty** of the **Delhi Sultanate**, was **Ala-Ud-Din Alam Shah**.

Upon ascending the throne in 1445 AD, he assumed the title of **Alam Shah**. Prior to taking this royal title, he was known as **Ala-Ud-Din**.

The confusion regarding the name **Hissan Khan** often arises in historical texts due to misinterpretations of his early titles or family lineage, but **Ala-Ud-Din Shah** is the historically recognized name for the Sultan before his coronation.

**Key points to remember:**
* The **Sayyid Dynasty** ruled from 1414 to 1451 AD.
* **Alam Shah** was the son of **Muhammad Shah**.
* He abdicated the throne in 1451 in favor of **Bahlul Lodi**, which marked the end of the Sayyid Dynasty and the beginning of the **Lodi Dynasty**.

Options like **Hamid Khan** and **Sarwar-Ul Mulk** were prominent officials and wazirs during the Sayyid period, but they were not the names of the Sultan himself.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Name the noted Mathematician, Astronomer of the Gupta period.
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **Aryabhata**. He was the most prominent mathematician and astronomer during the **Gupta period**, often referred to as the Golden Age of India.

**Aryabhata** authored the famous treatise **Aryabhatiya**, which covers significant astronomical and mathematical concepts. His major contributions include:

*   Calculating the value of π (Pi) as approximately 3.1416.
*   Proposing that the Earth rotates on its own axis and revolves around the Sun.
*   Explaining the scientific causes of **solar and lunar eclipses**, correctly identifying them as shadows cast by the Earth and Moon.
*   Advancing the use of **place value system** and the concept of zero.

Regarding the other options provided:

*   **Vatsyayana** was a philosopher and writer, most famous for authoring the **Kamasutra**.
*   **Varahamitra** was an astronomer and polymath who lived during the Gupta period, but he is distinct from Aryabhata. He is well-known for his work **Brihat Samhita**.
*   **Kalidasa** was a renowned **Sanskrit poet** and playwright, celebrated for works like **Abhijnanashakuntalam** and **Meghaduta**, rather than being a mathematician or astronomer.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q:
Match : [Post Name - Nature of Work]
A) Qaziul Quzat - 1) Chief City Magistrate
B) Mugaddam - 2) Legal Interpreter
C) Mufti - 3) Chief Justice
D) Amir-i-dadh - 4) Village Headman
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct matching is **A-3, B-4, C-2, D-1**. Here is the breakdown of these historical administrative titles used during the **Delhi Sultanate** and the **Mughal Empire**:

*   **Qaziul Quzat (A-3):** This title refers to the **Chief Justice** of the state. The individual holding this position was the highest judicial authority in the empire.

*   **Mugaddam (B-4):** This was a common term for the **Village Headman**. Their primary responsibility was the collection of land revenue and maintaining law and order at the local village level.

*   **Mufti (C-2):** A Mufti acted as a **Legal Interpreter**. They were scholars of Islamic law who provided rulings or interpretations known as *fatwas* to assist the Qazi in delivering justice.

*   **Amir-i-dadh (D-1):** This official served as the **Chief City Magistrate** or an officer of the high court. They were responsible for enforcing the law and ensuring the judgments of the Qazi were carried out, especially in urban centers.

Option 1 is correct because it accurately pairs the judicial and administrative roles with their traditional definitions. Other options fail because they swap these specialized functions incorrectly.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q:
Reason and Assertion type :
Assertion [A] : Ala-ud-din sent Zafar Khan and Ulugh Khan against the Mongols.
Reason [R] : The Mongols were defeated and Zafar Khan made the rules of Mongols.
options: Both are true But [R] is not the correct explanation of [A]
Both [A] and [R] are True and [R] is the correct explanation of [A]
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct option is 1.

**Assertion [A] is true** because **Ala-ud-din Khalji** did indeed dispatch his trusted generals, **Zafar Khan** and **Ulugh Khan**, to repel the constant **Mongol invasions** that threatened the Delhi Sultanate during his reign. They were instrumental in several key battles against the invaders.

**Reason [R] is false** because while Zafar Khan was a legendary warrior often called the "Rustam of the Age" for his bravery, he did not "make the rules of Mongols." Although he dealt heavy blows to the Mongol forces, he actually died in battle while fighting against the Mongol commander Qutlugh Khwaja.

The Mongols were defeated in various skirmishes, but they were never subjected to rules created by Zafar Khan. The assertion correctly identifies the historical military strategy of Ala-ud-din, but the stated reason is factually incorrect and misrepresents the nature of the conflict.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q:
Which of the following inscriptions belong to Samudragupta?
I) Allahabad Pillar Inscription
II) Nalanda Copper Plate
III) Eran Stone Inscription
IV) Mehruauli Pillar Inscription
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **I, II and III**.

The **Allahabad Pillar Inscription** (also known as the **Prayag Prashasti**) is the most famous source for the reign of **Samudragupta**. It was composed by his court poet **Harishena** and provides a detailed account of his military conquests and personal virtues.

The **Nalanda Copper Plate** and the **Eran Stone Inscription** also belong to Samudragupta. These inscriptions help historians map the extent of his empire and his administrative policies.

The **Mehrauli Pillar Inscription**, however, belongs to **Chandragupta II** (also known as Chandragupta Vikramaditya). It is famous for its high-quality iron craftsmanship that has resisted corrosion for centuries.

Since statement **IV** refers to the Mehrauli Pillar, any option containing it is incorrect. Therefore, the group including the first three inscriptions is the only accurate set.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: During the rule of the Khalji dynasty, the merchants had to bring all their goods for sale to
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
Under the reign of **Alauddin Khalji**, the **Sarai-e-Adl** was established as a centralized marketplace for manufactured goods and items imported from outside Delhi.

To ensure price control and market regulation, the Sultan mandated that all merchants bring their goods to this specific government-regulated market. This move was part of his broader **market reforms** designed to maintain a large standing army at low costs.

Here is why the other options are incorrect in this context:

* **Karkhana**: These were state-run workshops that manufactured luxury items and weapons for the royal household and army, not a public market for general merchants.
* **Kotwal**: This refers to the **Officer-in-Charge** of the city police and market administration who ensured the Sultan's regulations were followed, rather than the marketplace itself.
* **Igta**: This represents the administrative land grant system where assigned governors collected revenue to maintain troops, which is unrelated to trade centers.

The **Sarai-e-Adl** served as the hub for essential commodities like cloth, sugar, dried fruits, and herbs, all of which were sold at strictly fixed prices under royal supervision.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q: Among the Gupta rulers who adopted the title “Maharajadhiraja”?
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct answer is **Chandra Gupta - I**.

Historical records indicate that the early rulers of the **Gupta Dynasty**, specifically **Sree Gupta** and **Ghatotkacha**, were known simply by the title **Maharaja**. This title suggests they were local chieftains or feudatories rather than sovereign emperors.

**Chandra Gupta - I** was the first ruler of the dynasty to elevate his status significantly. By marrying the Lichchhavi princess **Kumara Devi**, he expanded his power and influence.

To signify his transition from a local chieftain to an independent and powerful sovereign, he adopted the grand title **Maharajadhiraja**, which translates to **King of Kings**.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

* **Sree Gupta**: He was the founder of the dynasty and used the modest title of **Maharaja**.
* **Samudra Gupta**: While he was a powerful emperor who held the title **Maharajadhiraja**, he was the successor to Chandra Gupta - I, not the first to adopt it.
* **Kumara Gupta**: He was a later ruler who continued the use of imperial titles established by his predecessors, such as **Mahendraditya**.

Remembering the sequence of titles helps distinguish the growth of the **Gupta Empire** from a small kingdom in Magadha to a vast sub-continental power.

questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.q:
Assertion [A] : In 1299, Ala-ud-din Khalji decided to capture Malwa and Gujarat and sent a large army under two of his generals.
Reason [R] : He had strong reasons for this expedition, as not only were these areas fertile and populous, but also controlled the Western Sea-Ports and Trade-Routes connecting them with Ganga valley.
options: Both [A] and [R] are true and [R] explains [A]
Both [A] and [R] are true but [R] does not explain [A]
questions/tm-history-guptas-and-delhi-su.explanation:
The correct option is 1. Both [A] and [R] are true and [R] explains [A].
