**Akbar** dispatched his forces under the command of **Mirza Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khanan** to annex **Sindh** into the **Mughal Empire**.

Here is the step-wise breakdown of the conquest:

*   The campaign was initiated in **1590** to bring the **Arghun** dynasty under Mughal control.
*   The decisive military operations took place in **1591**, leading to the submission of **Mirza Jani Beg**, the ruler of Sindh.
*   Following this victory, Sindh was formally integrated into the administrative structure of the empire as a province under the **Subah** system.

**1591** is the historically recognized year when the region successfully came under Mughal administration. Other dates provided in the options are incorrect because they do not align with the established timeline of the **Mughal expansion** into the Indus Valley.

The correct answer is **Doctor**. In the context of traditional medicine and historical terminology, **Hakim** refers to a physician or a wise man who practices Unani medicine. The term is widely used in South Asia and the Middle East to identify a medical practitioner.

*   **King** is incorrect because the term for a ruler or monarch is typically *Raja* or *Sultan*.
*   **Lawyer** is incorrect as a legal professional is referred to as a *Vakeel*.
*   **Scientist** is incorrect because it describes a modern profession focused on systematic study, whereas a *Hakim* focuses on traditional healing.

**Related Facts:**
*   The **Unani** system of medicine has its roots in ancient Greek philosophy.
*   A *Hakim* often utilizes herbal remedies and holistic approaches to treat ailments.

The correct year for the capture of **Golkonda** is **1687**.

The Mughal Emperor **Aurangzeb** personally led the campaign against the **Qutb Shahi dynasty**, which ruled Golkonda. After a long and arduous **eight-month siege**, the Mughal forces finally captured the Golkonda fort in **September 1687**.

This event marked the end of the **Qutb Shahi Kingdom** and its integration into the **Mughal Empire**. It was a significant strategic victory for Aurangzeb, as it allowed him to consolidate his control over the Deccan region.

The fall of Golkonda followed the annexation of **Bijapur**, which occurred earlier in the same year, in 1686. Together, these conquests effectively dismantled the major independent Sultanates of the Deccan.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-20.q: The english company secured madras in
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-20.explanation:
The correct answer is **1639**.

In **1639**, **Francis Day**, an agent of the **British East India Company**, obtained the grant of the site of **Madras** from the local ruler, the **Damarla Venkatapathy Nayak**, who was the representative of the **Vijayanagara Empire**.

Following this agreement, the British constructed **Fort St. George** on this land. This fortification became the nucleus around which the city of Madras (modern-day **Chennai**) grew and served as the administrative headquarters for the British in South India.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

*   **1612**: This year marks the establishment of the British factory at **Masulipatnam**, not Madras.
*   **1668**: This is the year when the British acquired **Bombay** from the Portuguese Crown as part of the dowry of Catherine of Braganza.
*   **1690**: This year is associated with the founding of **Calcutta** (Kolkata) by Job Charnock.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-20.q: Among these, who is English Trader
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-20.explanation:
The correct answer is **Peter Mundy**.

*   **Peter Mundy** was an English merchant and traveller who visited India during the reign of the Mughal Emperor **Shah Jahan** in the 17th century. His travelogues provide significant historical insights into the trade and social life of that era.

*   **Fahien** was a Chinese Buddhist monk who visited India during the reign of **Chandragupta II** (Gupta dynasty) in the 5th century. He traveled by land and sea to collect Buddhist scriptures.

*   **Francois Bernier** was a French physician and traveller who lived at the court of the Mughal Emperor **Aurangzeb**. His accounts are famous for detailing the economic and political conditions of 17th-century India from a European perspective.

*   **Al-Biruni** was a Persian scholar and polymath who accompanied **Mahmud of Ghazni** to India. He is known for writing the **Kitab-ul-Hind**, which is a seminal work on Indian culture, science, and philosophy in the 11th century.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-20.q: The english company secured Bombay in
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-20.explanation:
The British **East India Company** gained control of Bombay in **1668**.

Here is the historical context of this acquisition:

*   **Dowry Agreement**: Bombay was originally a Portuguese possession. It was given to the British King **Charles II** in 1661 as part of his dowry upon marrying the Portuguese Princess **Catherine of Braganza**.
*   **Royal Transfer**: King Charles II did not find the territory profitable to manage directly. Consequently, he leased the island of Bombay to the **East India Company** for a nominal annual rent of **10 pounds** in gold.
*   **The Date**: The formal transfer of the island to the Company took place in **1668**.

Option 3 (1687) is often confused with this event because that is the year the Company shifted its headquarters from **Surat** to **Bombay**. Since the question asks when the Company *secured* or acquired the island, **1668** is the historically accurate choice.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-20.q: When Would the French set up factories at surat in?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-20.explanation:
The **French East India Company** (*Compagnie des Indes Orientales*) was established under the initiative of **Jean-Baptiste Colbert** during the reign of King **Louis XIV**.

Following their arrival in India, the French focused on establishing trading posts to compete with other European powers. The timeline of their expansion is as follows:

*   The **first French factory** in India was established at **Surat** in **1668** by **Francois Caron**.
*   This was made possible after they received permission from the Mughal Emperor **Aurangzeb**.

Regarding the options provided, **1668** is the historically accurate year for the establishment of the Surat factory. While some historical records discuss later developments, 1668 remains the standard answer for the formal founding of their first Indian base.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-20.q: Sher shah built a new walled city in
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-20.explanation:
The correct answer is **Delhi**.

**Sher Shah Suri**, the founder of the **Sur Empire**, is well-known for his architectural contributions. During his brief reign between 1540 and 1545, he undertook the construction of a new fortified city.

This city was known as **Shergarh** (or the city of Sher Shah). It was built on the site of the ancient city of **Indraprastha** in **Delhi**.

The most prominent surviving structure from this project is the **Purana Qila** (Old Fort). He also built the famous **Qila-i-Kuhna Mosque** inside the fort complex, which is a fine example of his transition toward Mughal-style architecture.

**Key points to remember:**
* **Sher Shah Suri** is also famous for constructing the **Grand Trunk Road** and introducing the **Rupiya** as a silver currency.
* While the Mughals later developed their own capital cities, Sher Shah's construction at Delhi significantly shaped the city's urban landscape.
* **Agra** and **Pune** were not the primary focus of his new walled city projects, making them incorrect in this context.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-20.q: Humayun Defeating the Afghans at Daurah in?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-20.explanation:
The correct year for the **Battle of Daurah** (also known as the Battle of Dadrah) is **1532**.

Here is the breakdown of why this is the correct historical timeline:

*   **Humayun** ascended the throne following the death of his father, **Babur**, in **1530**.
*   Shortly after his accession, Humayun faced opposition from the **Afghans** led by **Mahmud Lodi**, who sought to regain control in the eastern regions.
*   In **1532**, Humayun marched against these Afghan forces and achieved a decisive victory at **Daurah**, located near Lucknow.

Regarding the other options:

*   **1470** is far too early, as it predates the arrival of the Mughals in India.
*   **1530** marks the year of Humayun's coronation, not his military engagement at Daurah.
*   **1539** is the year of the **Battle of Chausa**, where Humayun was defeated by **Sher Shah Suri**, leading to his temporary loss of the empire.

This victory at Daurah solidified Humayun's position early in his reign, though his struggle against the Afghan resurgence continued throughout the 1530s.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-20.q: A new Walled city was also known as __________
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-20.explanation:
The correct term for the "new walled city" established by **Humayun** and further developed by **Sher Shah Suri** is **Dinpanah**. However, in the context of your provided options, **Purana Qila** (The Old Fort) is the historical site associated with this city.

The site is famously known as the **Purana Qila** in Delhi. It was built on the legendary site of **Indraprastha**, the capital of the Pandavas in the Mahabharata.

Here is why the other options do not fit:

*   **Panch Mahal**: This is a five-storied architectural structure located in **Fatehpur Sikri**, commissioned by Emperor **Akbar**, not a walled city.
*   **Purana Hill**: This is not a standard historical name for the city; it is likely a misnomer for the fort site.
*   **Panch Qila**: This translates to "five forts" and is not recognized as the formal name for the city built by the Mughal or Sur dynasty rulers.

The **Purana Qila** remains one of the oldest forts in Delhi, serving as the citadel for the city of **Dinpanah**, which translates to the "Refuge of the Faithful."

The construction of the **Red Fort** (Lal Qila) in Delhi began in the year **1638**. It was commissioned by the Mughal Emperor **Shah Jahan** when he decided to shift his capital from **Agra** to **Shahjahanabad** (modern-day Old Delhi).

The project was massive and took nearly a decade to complete. The construction work officially concluded in **1648**, allowing the emperor to move into his new royal residence.

While the foundation was laid in 1638, the timeline is often summarized as 1638–1648. This structure served as the primary residence of the Mughal emperors for nearly 200 years until the fall of the empire in 1857.

The fort is renowned for its **red sandstone** walls and is a classic example of **Mughal architecture**, blending Persian, Timurid, and Hindu traditions. Today, it remains a site of great national significance, where the Prime Minister of India hoists the national flag every Independence Day.

**Sher Shah Suri**, the founder of the **Sur Empire** in northern India, met his end during the **Siege of Kalinjar**.

He died in **1545** due to an accidental explosion of gunpowder while he was besieging the fort of Kalinjar in Bundelkhand.

His death marked a significant turning point in medieval Indian history, as it halted the consolidation of the Sur dynasty. Following his death, his son **Islam Shah Suri** succeeded him to the throne.

*   **Sher Shah Suri** is best remembered for his administrative reforms and the construction of the **Grand Trunk Road**.
*   He also introduced the **Rupiya** as the standard currency, which served as the precursor to the modern **Rupee**.
*   His tomb is located in **Sasaram**, Bihar, and is considered a masterpiece of Indo-Islamic architecture.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-20.q: Who is the German Adventurer and traveller?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-20.explanation:
The correct answer is **Mandelslo**. **Johann Albrecht von Mandelslo** was a famous German traveler and adventurer who visited India during the 17th century.

He traveled extensively through the Mughal Empire and left detailed accounts of the social and political conditions of that era. His travelogues provide a unique European perspective on the administration and cultural life of the time.

* **Bernier** was a French physician and traveler.
* **Tavernier** was a French gem merchant and traveler.
* **Manucci** was an Italian traveler who served in the Mughal army.

Related Facts:
* Mandelslo visited the court of the Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan.
* His writings are highly valued by historians studying the 17th-century Indian subcontinent.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-21.q: Who is the French Physician and Traveller?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-21.explanation:
The correct answer is **François Bernier**.

He was a **French physician** and traveller who visited India during the **Mughal period**. He served as a personal physician to **Dara Shikoh**, the eldest son of Emperor Shah Jahan, and later remained in the court of **Aurangzeb**.

Here is why the other options are distinct:

* **Jean-Baptiste Tavernier** was a **French gem merchant** and traveller, famous for his extensive trade in diamonds and his travels to the East.
* **Johann Albrecht de Mandelslo** was a **German traveller** who visited the Mughal court during the reign of Shah Jahan.
* **Niccolao Manucci** was an **Italian writer** and traveller who arrived in India as a teenager and spent his life there, serving in the Mughal army.

Bernier's writings, specifically his work *Travels in the Mughal Empire*, provide deep insights into the social, economic, and political conditions of India during the 17th century. He is particularly noted for his detailed descriptions of the administrative structure and the comparison between European and Mughal systems.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-21.q: Who is the Italian Writer and Traveller
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-21.explanation:
**Niccolao Manucci** was an **Italian writer and traveller** who arrived in India during the reign of the Mughal Emperor **Shah Jahan**. He is best known for his extensive memoirs titled ***Storia do Mogor***, which provide a detailed account of the Mughal Empire.

Here is why the other options do not fit:

* **Bernier**: François Bernier was a **French physician** and traveller who spent many years at the court of Aurangzeb. He is famous for his work *Travels in the Mughal Empire*.
* **Tavernier**: Jean-Baptiste Tavernier was a **French gem merchant** and traveller. He made several journeys to India and is noted for his observations on the trade and economy of the time.
* **Mandelslo**: Johann Albrecht von Mandelslo was a **German traveller** who visited the Mughal Empire in the 17th century. His travelogues are significant for documenting the social conditions of the period.

**Manucci** holds a unique place in history because he served in the Mughal army and later as a physician, allowing him to witness the internal politics of the empire firsthand. His writings remain a vital source for historians studying the decline of the **Mughal Empire**.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-21.q: In which year the Jat Rebellion was held?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-21.explanation:
The **Jat Rebellion**, led by **Gokula**, began in the year **1669** during the reign of the Mughal Emperor **Aurangzeb**.

This uprising was primarily a result of the oppressive policies implemented by the Mughal administration, specifically in the **Mathura** region.

The conflict was sparked by the repressive actions of the local Mughal faujdar, **Abd-un-Nabi**, which provoked the local agrarian community.

The rebellion gained significant momentum in **1669** when the Jat peasants attacked and killed the faujdar, leading to a direct confrontation with the Mughal imperial forces.

Although the rebellion was eventually suppressed and **Gokula** was captured and executed in 1670, the year **1669** marks the historical commencement of this significant agrarian revolt against Mughal authority.

The correct answer is **Peter Mundy**, which corresponds to option 2 in the provided list.

**Peter Mundy** was a notable English traveler and merchant who visited India during the 17th century, specifically during the reign of the Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan. His writings provide valuable insights into the trade and social conditions of that era.

Here is why the other options are not English traders:

* **Mandelslo** was a German traveler who visited the Mughal court.
* **Manucci** was an Italian writer and adventurer who served in the Mughal army for many years.
* **Bernier** was a French physician and traveler who spent time at the court of Aurangzeb.

While the provided key suggests option 1, historical records identify **Peter Mundy** as the primary English merchant-traveler among these figures. His work, *Travels in Europe and Asia*, serves as a key primary source for historians studying the economic history of the **East India Company**.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-21.q: Who introduced the Zabt land revenue system during the Mughal era?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-21.explanation:
The correct answer is **Raja Todar Mal**.

The **Zabt system**, also known as the **Dahshala system**, was a sophisticated land revenue administration introduced by **Akbar** in 1580. While Akbar was the emperor who implemented it, **Raja Todar Mal**, his Finance Minister (**Diwan-i-Ashraf**), was the mastermind behind its design and execution.

Here is why this system was revolutionary:

*   It was based on the average produce of different crops and the average prices of the last **ten years**.
*   The land was surveyed and measured using standardized units, primarily the **jarib** (a bamboo pole with iron rings).
*   The revenue was fixed in cash rather than kind, which provided stability to the state treasury and reduced peasant exploitation.

Regarding the other options:

*   **Akbar** is often credited with the system, but **Raja Todar Mal** is the specific individual who devised the technical framework and served as the chief architect of Mughal revenue policy.
*   **Babar** and **Humayun** reigned during the early phase of the Mughal Empire and primarily followed older, less organized revenue practices.

This system was so effective that it became the backbone of Mughal fiscal stability and was later adopted by many regional rulers in India.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-21.q: The Zabt System was promulgated by Whom?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-21.explanation:
The correct answer is **Akbar**.

**Akbar** introduced the **Zabt system**, also known as the **Dahshala system**, to reform the land revenue administration of his empire. He implemented this system with the expertise of his finance minister, **Raja Todar Mal**.

Under this system, the land was measured, and the revenue was fixed based on the average production and prices of crops over the past ten years. This provided stability and transparency to the farmers and the state.

*   **Babar** was the founder of the Mughal Empire and focused on establishing his rule.
*   **Humayun** spent most of his reign struggling to maintain his territory rather than introducing major administrative reforms.
*   While **Raja Todar Mal** was the architect who executed the system, the system itself was promulgated and authorized under the reign and authority of **Akbar**.

**Related Facts:**
*   The **Zabt system** covered provinces like Lahore, Multan, Delhi, Agra, Allahabad, and Malwa.
*   It classified land into four categories: **Polaj**, **Parauti**, **Chachar**, and **Banjar**.

**Faizi** is the correct answer. He was a distinguished scholar, poet, and mathematician in the court of **Akbar**.

Here is why he holds this title:

*   Faizi was the elder brother of the famous historian **Abul Fazl**.
*   He was appointed as the **Malik-ush-Shu'ara** (Poet Laureate) by Akbar.
*   He played a significant role in translating famous **Sanskrit** works like the *Mahabharata* and *Bhagavad Gita* into **Persian**.

Other options explained:

*   **Peter Mundy** was a European traveler who visited India during the reign of Shah Jahan, not Akbar.
*   **Raja Todar Mal** was Akbar’s talented **Finance Minister**, famous for introducing the *Dahsala* land revenue system.
*   **Akbar** was the **Mughal Emperor** himself, not a court poet.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-21.q: Bhaskaracharya's famous work leelavati was translated by Whom?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-21.explanation:
The correct answer is **Faizi**.

**Bhaskaracharya**, a renowned 12th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer, authored **Leelavati**, which is a seminal treatise on arithmetic and geometry.

During the Mughal period, the Persian scholar **Abul-Fazl ibn Mubarak**, popularly known as **Faizi**, translated the work into Persian at the command of Emperor **Akbar**. This translation played a significant role in spreading Indian mathematical knowledge throughout the Islamic world.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

*   **Aryabhatta** was a much earlier mathematician known for the **Aryabhatiya**, predating Bhaskaracharya by several centuries.
*   **Dhanvantri** is traditionally revered as a physician and is associated with the field of **Ayurveda**, not the translation of mathematical texts.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-21.q: In mughals period, how will the domestic traders were called?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-21.explanation:
The correct answer is **Seth**.

During the Mughal period, the internal trade of the empire was carried out by various merchant groups. The **Seth** were prominent domestic traders and bankers who held significant influence in the economic structure of the time.

Other terms refer to different roles or groups:
* **Bora** refers to a specific community of traders, often associated with the Dawoodi Bohra sect.
* **Panik** is not a standard term for domestic traders in this context.
* **Pancharas** (Banjaras) were primarily **itinerant grain merchants** who transported goods across the country using bullock caravans, rather than stationary domestic traders.

Related Facts:
* The Mughals encouraged trade by building extensive road networks and sarais.
* The **Hundi** or bill of exchange was widely used by these traders to conduct financial transactions across long distances.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-21.q: In mughals period, how will the Foreign traders were called?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-21.explanation:
The correct answer is **Bora**.

During the Mughal period, the term **Bora** was specifically used to refer to foreign traders, particularly those belonging to the merchant communities involved in long-distance trade. These traders played a vital role in the economic network of the empire by facilitating the exchange of goods between different regions.

While **Seth** refers to a wealthy merchant or banker in a general sense within the Indian context, it does not specifically define foreign traders as the term **Bora** does. **Pancharas** were primarily nomadic transporters of goods rather than foreign traders.

Related Facts:
* The **Bora** community remains a significant mercantile group in India today.
* Mughal trade flourished due to the presence of these organized merchant guilds.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-22.q: In mughals period, how will the Wholesale traders were called?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-22.explanation:
During the Mughal period, the commercial landscape was highly organized, featuring distinct categories of merchants based on the scale of their trade.

The term **Banik** (often referred to as **Banias**) was used to identify the **wholesale traders** and merchant guilds who managed large-scale distribution of goods across various regions.

Here is why the other terms differ in context:

*   **Seth** (or Sahukar): These were typically the **wealthy bankers** or money-lenders who provided credit and financial services to the state and merchants.
*   **Bohra**: This group primarily consisted of merchants engaged in **overseas trade** and maritime commerce, particularly along the western coast of India.
*   **Pancharas**: This term does not represent a specific category of wholesale traders within the historical administrative or economic documents of the Mughal era.

The **Baniks** played a crucial role in the Mughal economy by linking the rural producers with urban markets and facilitating the movement of textiles, spices, and food grains. Their extensive network of agents and warehouses helped sustain the vast trade routes of the 16th and 17th centuries.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-22.q: Babur came to India originally from
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-22.explanation:
The correct answer is **Ferghana**.

**Babur**, the founder of the **Mughal Empire** in India, was a descendant of both **Genghis Khan** and **Timur**. He was born in **1483** in **Ferghana**, a small principality located in present-day **Uzbekistan**.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

*   **Khorasan** was a historical region in Central Asia that Babur moved through during his various campaigns, but it was not his place of origin.
*   **Khilar** is not a relevant geographical origin for Babur in the context of historical records.

After losing his ancestral throne in **Ferghana** due to internal conflicts and rivals, Babur spent years wandering before capturing **Kabul** in 1504. From Kabul, he launched his successful military campaigns into the Indian subcontinent, eventually defeating **Ibrahim Lodi** at the **First Battle of Panipat** in **1526**.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-22.q: Akbar was enthroned in a garden at
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-22.explanation:
**Akbar** was enthroned at **Kalanaur** in the year **1556** AD.

At the time of his father **Humayun's** sudden death, Akbar was only 13 years old and was stationed in the Punjab region.

His guardian, **Bairam Khan**, organized the coronation ceremony on a simple brick platform at **Kalanaur** (located in present-day Gurdaspur district, Punjab). This event marked the beginning of his formal reign as the third **Mughal Emperor**.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

* **Ajmer** was an important strategic center and religious site for the Mughals, but it was not the location of his coronation.
* **Gaur** was a historic capital in Bengal, famously associated with earlier rulers, but it holds no significance regarding Akbar's enthronement.

Following the ceremony at **Kalanaur**, Akbar soon faced his greatest initial challenge, the **Second Battle of Panipat**, where he secured his throne against **Hemu**.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-22.q: Where did the French establish their first factory?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-22.explanation:
The correct answer is **Surat**.

The **French East India Company** was established in 1664 under the patronage of **Jean-Baptiste Colbert**, a minister under King Louis XIV.

Following their arrival in India, they sought permission from the Mughal Emperor to conduct trade. Consequently, the first French factory was successfully established at **Surat** in **1668** by **Francois Caron**.

**Surat** was the primary choice for many European powers, including the British and the Dutch, because it served as a major center for maritime trade and commerce in the 17th century.

*   **Agra** was an inland administrative hub rather than a coastal trading port for the French.
*   **Chennai** (Madras) became a significant French base only later, specifically after the capture of **Pondicherry** and the development of their southern influence.
*   **Mumbai** (Bombay) was primarily under the control of the British after it was received as part of a dowry by King Charles II.

After Surat, the French moved their focus to **Pondicherry**, which eventually became the headquarters of French power in India.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-22.q: In the Mughal administration, military recruitment had been looked after by the
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-22.explanation:
The correct official responsible for military recruitment and administration in the Mughal Empire was the **Mir Bakhshi**.

Here is why **Bakhshi** is the correct choice:

* The **Mir Bakhshi** served as the head of the military department. His primary duties included the recruitment of soldiers, the maintenance of the descriptive rolls of soldiers, and the inspection of horses.
* He also acted as the **Paymaster-General**, responsible for overseeing the payment of salaries to the military officers known as **Mansabdars**.
* Because he was the head of the military establishment and kept the official records of all military appointments, he was the central figure in military personnel management.

Why the other options are incorrect:

* The **Kotwal** was a local police officer responsible for maintaining law and order, public safety, and regulating markets within a city or town.
* The **Wazir** (often referred to as the **Vakil** or **Diwan-i-Ala**) was the chief financial officer or prime minister, responsible for the overall administration and state revenue.
* The **Diwan** was the head of the revenue department. His focus was primarily on state income, expenditure, and fiscal policies, rather than military recruitment.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-22.q: Which of the following Mughal emperors is credited with composition of Hindi songs?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-22.explanation:
The correct answer is **Jahangir**.

**Jahangir** is widely celebrated for his deep interest in arts, music, and poetry. Historians credit him with the composition of several Hindi songs, showcasing his command over the language and his patronage of local cultural traditions during the Mughal era.

*   **Akbar** is known for his policy of religious tolerance and administrative reforms, but not specifically for composing Hindi songs.
*   **Humayun** spent most of his reign struggling to stabilize his empire, leaving little time for literary compositions of this nature.
*   **Babur** is famous for his memoir, the **Baburnama**, written in the Chagatai Turkish language.

Related Facts:
*   **Jahangir** was a great connoisseur of painting and established a royal workshop for artists.
*   His memoirs, the **Tuzk-e-Jahangiri**, provide immense detail about his personal interests and the state of the empire.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-22.q: Who got the Gita translated into Persian?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-22.explanation:
The correct person responsible for the Persian translation of the **Bhagavad Gita** is **Dara Shikoh**. He was the eldest son of the Mughal Emperor **Shah Jahan** and a renowned scholar of comparative religion.

**Dara Shikoh** was deeply interested in the mystical aspects of different faiths. He believed that the **Upanishads** and the **Gita** shared a common monotheistic foundation with the **Quran**.

Under his patronage, a team of scholars translated several **Sanskrit** texts into Persian. His most famous work, the ***Sirr-i-Akbar***, is a collection of 50 Upanishads translated into Persian.

The translation of the **Gita** facilitated the study of Indian philosophy by Persian-speaking intellectuals. This initiative marked a significant effort in promoting religious harmony and cultural synthesis during the Mughal period.

Regarding the other options provided:
* **Akbar** is famous for establishing the ***Maktab Khana*** (Translation Bureau), where texts like the *Mahabharata* and *Ramayana* were translated into Persian, but he did not personally translate the Gita.
* **Humayun** and **Babar** were earlier Mughal rulers focused primarily on establishing the empire's political foundation rather than these specific philosophical translations.

The correct answer is **Sambhaji**. Aurangzeb dispatched **Mukarrab Khan** to lead the military campaign against the Maratha ruler **Sambhaji** in 1689. This campaign successfully led to the capture of Sambhaji at Sangameshwar.

Following his capture, Sambhaji was brought before the Mughal Emperor and executed, marking a significant turn in the Mughal-Maratha conflict. Other options are incorrect because:

* **Jahangir** was an earlier Mughal Emperor.
* **Shivaji** died in 1680, years before this specific campaign occurred.

Related Facts:
* Sambhaji was the eldest son of Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj.
* The conflict between the Mughals and Marathas, known as the Maratha War of Independence, lasted for 27 years.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-22.q: Which Mughal Emperor transferred the Mughal Capital from Agra to Delhi?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-22.explanation:
The correct answer is **Shah Jahan**.

While the provided option index suggests an earlier ruler, historical records confirm that **Shah Jahan** was the emperor responsible for shifting the capital.

In **1638**, Shah Jahan decided to move the Mughal capital from **Agra** to **Delhi**. He commissioned the construction of a new walled city named **Shahjahanabad**, which today is known as **Old Delhi**.

This move was driven by a desire to have a more strategically located capital and to build a grand city that reflected his architectural ambitions. The most famous structure within this new capital is the **Red Fort**, which served as the residence of the Mughal emperors.

To understand why the other options are incorrect:
* **Babar** founded the Mughal Empire but maintained his primary base in Agra.
* **Akbar** established **Fatehpur Sikri** as a capital for a short duration, but returned to Agra afterward.
* **Jahangir** continued to rule primarily from Agra and Lahore during his reign.

The reign of **Shah Jahan** is often referred to as the "Golden Age" of Mughal architecture due to his massive construction projects across Delhi, Agra, and Lahore.

The correct answer is **Gulbadan Begum**.

**Gulbadan Begum** was the daughter of the Mughal Emperor **Babur** and the half-sister of Emperor **Humayun**. She composed the **Humayun Nama** at the request of her nephew, **Akbar**, to document the life and times of his father.

This work is an invaluable historical source, as it provides a rare, intimate perspective on the Mughal royal household, social customs, and the political climate of that era.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

*   **Dara Shikoh** was the eldest son of Shah Jahan, known for his interest in comparative religion and philosophy, not for writing this biography.
*   **Akbar** commissioned the work but did not write it himself.
*   **Babur** is famous for writing his own autobiography, known as the **Baburnama** or **Tuzk-e-Baburi**.

The **Humayun Nama** remains one of the few historical accounts written by a woman during the Mughal period, making it a unique piece of literature.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-23.q: Who defeated Humayun in the battle of Chausa?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-23.explanation:
The correct answer is **Sher Shah Suri**.

The **Battle of Chausa** took place in **1539** between the Mughal Emperor **Humayun** and the Afghan ruler **Sher Shah Suri**.

Here is why this event is significant:

*   **Sher Shah Suri** successfully used military strategy to surprise and defeat the Mughal forces near the village of Chausa, located on the banks of the **Ganges river**.
*   Following this victory, **Sher Shah** declared himself an independent ruler and assumed the title of **Shah**.
*   This defeat was a major setback for **Humayun**, and he was eventually forced to flee towards Agra.

To understand why the other options are incorrect:

*   **Feroz Shah** refers to rulers from the Tughlaq dynasty who lived long before the Mughal-Sur conflict.
*   **Shivaji** was the legendary founder of the **Maratha Empire** and operated in the 17th century, well after the time of Humayun.
*   **Dara Shikoh** was the eldest son of the Mughal Emperor **Shah Jahan** and lived during the 17th century.

One year after Chausa, in **1540**, **Sher Shah Suri** defeated **Humayun** again at the **Battle of Kannauj** (also known as the Battle of Bilgram), which led to the temporary collapse of the Mughal Empire and the establishment of the **Sur Empire**.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-23.q: Who constructed Humayun’s tomb in Delhi?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-23.explanation:
The construction of **Humayun’s Tomb** in Delhi was commissioned by his widow, **Haji Begum**, who is also known as **Bega Begum**. She supervised the project after the emperor's death.

The architectural design was carried out by the Persian architect **Mirak Mirza Ghiyas**. This structure is widely recognized as the first garden-tomb on the Indian subcontinent.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

* **Akbar**: He was the son of Humayun. While he oversaw the reign during which the tomb was completed, he was not the primary patron who commissioned the construction.
* **Shah Jahan**: He is famous for building the Taj Mahal, which was heavily influenced by the architectural style of Humayun's Tomb, but he lived much later.
* **Dara Shikoh**: He was a later Mughal prince and a son of Shah Jahan, known for his interest in philosophy and religious syncretism, not for the construction of this monument.

**Humayun's Tomb** is a landmark in **Mughal architecture**, being the first building in India to use the **double dome** technique and the **charbagh** (four-fold garden) layout. It serves as a precursor to the style eventually perfected in the Taj Mahal.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-23.q: The Mansabdari system introduced by Akbar was borrowed from the system prevalent in
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-23.explanation:
The **Mansabdari system** was a unique administrative and military grading system implemented by **Akbar** to organize his bureaucracy and army.

The system was primarily inspired by the military organization of the **Mongols**. Specifically, it was derived from the decimal system of military grading used by **Genghis Khan**, where the army was divided into units of 10, 100, 1,000, and 10,000 soldiers.

While the Mughal administration adopted various Persian cultural and linguistic influences due to the dynasty's Central Asian roots, the structural framework of the **Mansab** (rank) was a direct adaptation of the Mongol military traditions.

* **Mongolia**: Correct. It reflects the decimal organizational structure common in Mongol military history.
* **Afghanistan**: Incorrect. While the Mughals had connections to Afghanistan, the specific structural origin of the military rank system was not derived from there.
* **Persia**: Incorrect. Although Persian influences were strong in the Mughal court, language, and culture, the Mansabdari structure is historically attributed to the Mongol legacy.
* **China**: Incorrect. There is no historical evidence linking the Mansabdari system to the administrative models of ancient or contemporary China.

Under this system, every official was assigned a **Mansab**, which determined their status, salary, and the number of **Sawar** (cavalrymen) they were required to maintain. This system proved effective in consolidating the power of the Mughal Empire for over a century.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-23.q: Which Rajput dynasty had not surrendered to Akbar?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-23.explanation:
The correct answer is the **Sisodiya** dynasty of **Mewar**.

*   **Akbar’s** expansionist policy sought the submission of all major Rajput kingdoms to the **Mughal Empire**.
*   The **Sisodiya** rulers of Mewar, led notably by **Maharana Pratap**, famously refused to accept the suzerainty of Akbar.
*   This defiance led to the historic **Battle of Haldighati** in 1576, where Maharana Pratap continued his resistance rather than surrendering or entering into a matrimonial alliance with the Mughals.

Regarding the other options:

*   **Pratiharas** (Gurjara-Pratiharas) were a significant power in northern India long before the Mughal era, typically associated with the medieval period between the 8th and 11th centuries.
*   **Parmars** (Paramaras) were a prominent dynasty that ruled the Malwa region much earlier, reaching their peak under Raja Bhoj in the 11th century.
*   **Rathors** (Rathores) of Marwar (Jodhpur) eventually aligned with the Mughals and provided significant military service to the empire, unlike the Sisodiyas who maintained their independent stance.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-23.q: The architectural raw material generally used in Akbar’s period was
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-23.explanation:
The correct answer is **Red Sandstone**.

**Akbar's architectural style** is famously characterized by the extensive use of **Red Sandstone** as the primary building material. This can be clearly observed in monumental structures like **Fatehpur Sikri**, the **Agra Fort**, and **Humayun's Tomb**.

While marble was used in later Mughal architecture—particularly during the reign of **Shah Jahan**, who preferred white marble—it was utilized only sparingly during Akbar's time, often just for inlay work or decorative borders.

Here is why the other options are less significant in this context:

* **Marble Stone**: This became the hallmark of the later Mughal period, especially under Shah Jahan (e.g., the Taj Mahal).
* **Brick**: While used for core construction, it was almost always faced with sandstone to provide the grand, reddish aesthetic typical of the era.
* **Limestone**: Generally used as mortar or a binding agent rather than the primary architectural material for exterior facades.

The **Mughal transition** from the earlier Afghan style to the refined Akbar style was largely defined by this signature use of **Red Sandstone**, which provided a bold and uniform texture to his empire's grand structures.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-23.q: During Akbar’s reign, who was the Finance Minister of the Mughal empire?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-23.explanation:
The correct person who served as the **Finance Minister** (Diwan-i-Ashraf) during the reign of **Akbar** was **Raja Todar Mal**.

He was a brilliant administrator and one of the **Navaratnas** (Nine Gems) in Akbar’s court. He is best known for implementing the **Dahshala system**, also known as the **Zabti system**, which revolutionized land revenue collection.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

*   **Akbar** was the Mughal Emperor himself, not the minister in charge of finance.
*   **Babar** was the founder of the Mughal Empire and the grandfather of Akbar, predating Akbar's reign significantly.
*   **Humayun** was Akbar's father and the second Mughal Emperor, who preceded Akbar on the throne.

**Raja Todar Mal's** reforms involved surveying the land and fixing revenue based on the average yield of crops over the previous ten years. This systematic approach ensured a stable income for the empire and provided relief to the peasantry by standardizing tax rates.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-23.q: Which was the second capital of Akbar?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-23.explanation:
The correct answer is **Fatehpur Sikri**. While the declared option was incorrect, historically, Akbar shifted his capital from **Agra** to **Fatehpur Sikri** in 1571 to honor the Sufi saint **Salim Chishti**.

Here is why **Fatehpur Sikri** is the right choice:

* **Strategic Planning**: Akbar built this city specifically to serve as his new administrative center. It remained the capital from 1571 to 1585.
* **Architectural Marvel**: It is renowned for structures like the **Buland Darwaza**, **Panch Mahal**, and the **Diwan-i-Khas**, showcasing a blend of Hindu and Persian architectural styles.
* **Reason for Relocation**: The city was eventually abandoned around 1585, primarily due to a severe **shortage of water** in the region.

Regarding the other options:

* **Agra** served as the primary capital during the early years of Akbar's reign.
* **Delhi** was the traditional seat of the Mughal Empire, but it was not the specific "second capital" established by Akbar.
* **Pune** has no historical connection to the Mughal capital system under Akbar.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-23.q: Akbar saw the sea for the first time in his life at
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-23.explanation:
The correct answer is **Cambay**.

Historical accounts from the reign of **Akbar the Great** indicate that he first witnessed the sea during his military campaign in **Gujarat** in **1573**.

Following the surrender of the fortress at **Surat**, Akbar moved toward **Cambay** (modern-day Khambhat). It was at this location that he reached the shores of the **Arabian Sea** for the very first time.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

* **Surat**: While Akbar captured the fort of Surat during this campaign, his first actual encounter with the sight of the sea occurred specifically when he reached the town of Cambay shortly thereafter.
* **Bombay**: During the 16th century, Bombay was merely a group of small islands controlled by the Sultanate of Gujarat and later the Portuguese; it was not a significant imperial destination for Akbar.
* **Kolkata**: Kolkata did not exist as a prominent city during Akbar's time; the region was part of the Bengal Sultanate, which was geographically distant from Akbar's western maritime experiences.

This event is well-documented in the **Akbarnama**, the official chronicle of Akbar's reign written by **Abul Fazl**, highlighting his curiosity and fascination upon seeing the vast expanse of the ocean.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-23.q: Who was the regent of Akbar in his early days?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-23.explanation:
The correct answer is **Bairam Khan**.

When **Akbar** ascended the throne in 1556 at the young age of thirteen, he was too inexperienced to govern the empire alone. **Bairam Khan**, a loyal general and mentor of his father **Humayun**, was appointed as his **Ataliq** or regent.

**Bairam Khan** played a crucial role in stabilizing the young emperor's rule. He was the primary military commander during the **Second Battle of Panipat** in 1556, where he defeated **Hemu**, the Hindu king who had captured Delhi.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

* **Humayun** was **Akbar's father** and the emperor preceding him; his death necessitated the appointment of a regent.
* **Raja Todar Mal** was a brilliant **Finance Minister** under Akbar's later administration, known for his land revenue system called **Dahshala**.
* **Sher Shah Suri** was the founder of the **Sur Empire** and a fierce rival of the Mughal dynasty, having defeated Humayun earlier in his career.

**Bairam Khan** acted as the de facto ruler of the Mughal Empire for about four years until **Akbar** grew old enough to assume full control of the government in 1560.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-23.q: Which Book provides extremely rich and interesting details about the social and cultural life in the subcontinent in the fourteenth century?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-23.explanation:
The correct answer is **Rihala**.

This travelogue was written by the famous Moroccan traveler **Ibn Battuta**, who visited India during the reign of **Muhammad bin Tughlaq** in the 14th century.

Here is why **Rihala** is significant:

* It provides a vivid, firsthand account of the political, social, and economic conditions of India under the **Delhi Sultanate**.
* Ibn Battuta documented details about trade routes, the postal system, and the customs of various Indian regions, making it a primary historical source.
* The term **Rihala** translates to "My Travels" and serves as a vital record of the medieval Islamic world.

Regarding the other options:

* **Arthashastra** was authored by **Chanakya** (Kautilya) in the 4th century BCE, focusing on statecraft and administration in the Mauryan period.
* **Discovery of India** is a modern work written by **Jawaharlal Nehru** during his imprisonment in the 1940s.
* **Dihal** is not a recognized historical text relevant to the social history of the 14th-century subcontinent.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-24.explanation:
**Francois Bernier** was a **French physician** and traveler who visited India during the 17th century.

He is best known for being a member of the court of the Mughal Emperor **Aurangzeb**.

He served as a personal physician to **Dara Shikoh**, the eldest son of Emperor Shah Jahan, and later became associated with the imperial court.

His written work, **Travels in the Mughal Empire**, provides an extensive and detailed account of the political, social, and economic life in India during that period.

Because he originated from **France**, the correct classification is **Frenchman**.

The other options are incorrect because he had no British or Indian nationality; he was a European observer documenting the Mughal administration for his home country.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-24.q: According to Ibn-Battuta, which city was the largest one?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-24.explanation:
The correct answer is **Delhi**.

According to **Ibn Battuta**, a famous Moroccan traveler who visited India during the reign of **Muhammad bin Tughlaq**, Delhi was the largest city in the entire Islamic East.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

* **Surat**, **Mumbai**, and **Chennai** were not prominent metropolitan centers during the medieval period of the **Delhi Sultanate**.
* **Surat** gained historical significance much later as a major port city during the **Mughal Empire** and colonial rule.
* **Mumbai** and **Chennai** were developed primarily by the British as presidencies long after Ibn Battuta’s journey in the 14^(th) century.

Ibn Battuta described Delhi as a city of vast extent and population, highlighting its grandeur, the strength of its fortifications, and the immense wealth of the Sultanate. He specifically noted that it was the greatest city in the Indian subcontinent at that time.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-24.q: Who wrote a detailed account of trade and society in south India?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-24.explanation:
The correct answer is **Duarte Barbosa**.

**Duarte Barbosa** was a Portuguese writer and officer who lived in India during the early 16th century. His work, titled *The Book of Duarte Barbosa*, provides a vivid and comprehensive account of the social customs, trade, and political conditions of the **Vijayanagara Empire** and other regions in south India.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

* **Ibn Battuta** was a Moroccan traveler who visited India during the reign of Muhammad bin Tughlaq in the 14th century, focusing primarily on the Delhi Sultanate rather than south Indian trade specifically.
* **Fahien** was a Chinese Buddhist monk who traveled to India during the Gupta period (specifically the reign of Chandragupta II) to collect Buddhist texts and visit holy sites.
* **Al-Biruni** was a Persian scholar who accompanied Mahmud of Ghazni; his famous work, *Tahqiq-i-Hind*, offers deep insights into Indian science, religion, and philosophy, but it predates the significant European accounts of south Indian maritime trade.

**Duarte Barbosa**'s account is uniquely valuable because it details the bustling commerce of ports like **Calicut** and **Cochin**, documenting how spice trade linked India to global markets during the early colonial era.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-24.q: Which Traveller spent several years travelling through north Africa, West Asia and parts of Central Asia (he may even have visited Russia), the Indian subcontinent and China?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-24.explanation:
The correct answer is **Ibn Battuta**.

**Ibn Battuta** was a renowned Moroccan scholar and explorer born in **Tangier**. In the 14th century, he embarked on a journey that lasted nearly **30 years**, covering approximately **75,000 miles**.

His travels spanned the **Islamic world** and beyond, including:
*   **North Africa** and the **Middle East** (West Asia).
*   **Central Asia** and parts of the **Golden Horde** (Russia).
*   The **Indian Subcontinent**, where he served as a *Qazi* (judge) in the court of **Muhammad bin Tughlaq** for several years.
*   **China** and Southeast Asia.

He documented these extensive travels in his famous travelogue titled **Rihla** (The Journey). This book remains a crucial historical source for understanding the social, political, and cultural conditions of the 14th-century world.

Why the other options do not fit:
*   **Fahien** was a Chinese Buddhist monk who visited India during the Gupta period, primarily focusing on his religious pilgrimage.
*   **Francois Bernier** was a French physician and traveler who visited India much later, specifically during the reign of **Aurangzeb**.
*   **Al-Biruni** was a Persian scholar who accompanied Mahmud of Ghazni to India and wrote the *Kitab-al-Hind*, but he did not undertake the vast, multi-continental travels characteristic of Ibn Battuta.

**Jean-Baptiste Tavernier** was a renowned French **gem merchant** and traveller during the 17th century. He is widely recognized in history for his extensive travels to India and the Mughal Empire.

The correct answer is **Jeweller**.

He is specifically famous for being one of the first Europeans to trade in precious stones and for his detailed journals describing the **Mughal court**. He is well known for purchasing the famous **Blue Diamond**, which was later recut to become the **Hope Diamond**.

His accounts provide invaluable insights into the economy, social structure, and royal lifestyle of India during the reign of **Shah Jahan** and **Aurangzeb**. Because he dealt extensively in diamonds and gemstones, his profession is strictly categorized as a **jeweller**.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-24.q: Padshah Namah was a biography of whom?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-24.explanation:
The **Padshah Namah** (Chronicle of the King of the World) is the official biography written to document the reign of the Mughal Emperor **Shah Jahan**.

The correct answer is **3**.

The work was commissioned by **Shah Jahan** himself and serves as a detailed historical account of his life and administration. It was authored by court historians, most notably **Abdul Hamid Lahori**.

*   **Content:** The text provides a vivid description of the grandeur of the Mughal court, military campaigns, and the construction of architectural marvels like the **Taj Mahal**.
*   **Artistic Value:** The manuscripts are famous for their exquisite **miniature paintings**, which illustrate scenes from the emperor's life and court events.
*   **Clarification:** While other emperors had their own biographies—such as the **Baburnama** for Babur and the **Akbarnama** for Akbar—the **Padshah Namah** is exclusively dedicated to the reign of **Shah Jahan**.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-24.q: Babur Nama was a biography of whom?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-24.explanation:
The correct answer is **Babar**.

**Babur Nama**, also known as **Tuzk-e-Babri**, is the authentic **autobiography** of **Zahir-ud-din Muhammad Babur**, the founder of the **Mughal Empire** in India.

It is a significant historical document because:

*   It was originally written in **Chaghatai Turkic**, which was Babur's mother tongue.
*   It provides a detailed, honest, and firsthand account of his life, his military campaigns in Central Asia and India, and his personal observations on nature, flora, and fauna.
*   Later, during the reign of **Akbar**, the work was translated into **Persian** by Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khanan, which helped preserve it for future historians.

Regarding the other options:

*   **Fahien** was a Chinese pilgrim who visited India during the Gupta period, long before the Mughal era.
*   **Akbar** and **Shah Jahan** were later Mughal emperors whose lives were chronicled by court historians in works like the **Akbarnama** and **Padshahnama**, rather than their own autobiographies.

The correct answer is **Guru Har Gobind**.

**Guru Har Gobind** served as the 6th Sikh Guru from 1606 to 1644. He is famously known as the *Miri-Piri* Guru because he introduced the concept of both temporal (worldly) and spiritual authority to the Sikh community.

He transformed the Sikh community into a martial force to defend against persecution. He built the **Akal Takht** and encouraged Sikhs to engage in physical training and martial arts.

* **Guru Arjun Dev** was the 5th Guru.
* **Guru Tej Bahadur** was the 9th Guru.
* **Guru Shar Roy** is not a historical figure among the ten Sikh Gurus.

Related Facts:
* He was the son of Guru Arjun Dev.
* He was the first Guru to start the tradition of wearing two swords.

The 7th Guru of the Sikhs is **Guru Har Rai**.

In the provided options, **Guru Har Bahadur** is a misnomer for **Guru Har Rai**. He served as the leader of the Sikh community from 1644 to 1661.

Here is the chronological order of the early Sikh Gurus for your reference:
1. Guru Nanak Dev
2. Guru Angad Dev
3. Guru Amar Das
4. Guru Ram Das
5. Guru Arjan Dev
6. Guru Har Gobind
7. **Guru Har Rai**

**Guru Har Rai** was known for his peaceful nature and his focus on maintaining a large army to ensure the community's defense, though he avoided direct military conflict. He was the grandson of the 6th Guru, **Guru Har Gobind**.

Regarding the other names mentioned:
* **Guru Arjan Dev** was the 5th Guru and is famous for compiling the **Adi Granth**.
* **Guru Tegh Bahadur** was the 9th Guru, who was martyred for his commitment to religious freedom.

"Guru Shar Roy" is not a historical figure within the lineage of the Sikh Gurus.

The 10th and final human Guru of the Sikhs is **Guru Gobind Singh**. He succeeded his father, **Guru Tegh Bahadur**, to become the spiritual and temporal leader of the Sikh community in 1675.

He is widely revered for several transformative contributions to Sikhism:

*   **Formation of the Khalsa**: In 1699, he established the **Khalsa Panth**, an order of initiated Sikhs committed to defending the faith and protecting the oppressed.
*   **The Five Ks**: He introduced the mandatory articles of faith known as the **Panj Kakar** (Kesh, Kangha, Kara, Kachera, and Kirpan) to distinguish the identity of the Khalsa.
*   **Guru Granth Sahib**: Before his passing, he declared the sacred scripture, the **Guru Granth Sahib**, as the eternal and living Guru for all Sikhs, ending the succession of human gurus.

Regarding the other options:

*   **Guru Arjun Dev** was the 5th Sikh Guru and is remembered for compiling the Adi Granth and building the Golden Temple.
*   **Guru Tegh Bahadur** (often mislabeled as Guru Har Bahadur) was the 9th Sikh Guru.
*   **Guru Shar Roy** is not a historical figure in the Sikh lineage.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-25.explanation:
The correct answer is **Guru Nanak**.

**Guru Nanak Dev Ji** was the founder of **Sikhism** and the first of the ten Sikh Gurus. He was born in 1469 in Talwandi, a village now known as Nankana Sahib in present-day Pakistan.

He preached the message of **oneness of God**, equality, and service to humanity. His teachings are preserved in the **Guru Granth Sahib**, which is the central religious scripture of Sikhism.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

* **Guru Tej Bahadur** was the 9th Sikh Guru, known for his sacrifice in defense of religious freedom.
* **Guru Har Gobind** (often referred to in similar contexts) was the 6th Sikh Guru, known for militarizing the Sikh community.
* **Guru Shar Roy** is not one of the ten historical Sikh Gurus.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-25.q: In 1453, Muhammad Gawan's arrival at which place?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-25.explanation:
**Muhammad Gawan**, a renowned statesman and scholar, arrived in India from Gilan in Persia in the year **1453**.

He arrived specifically at the **Bahmani Kingdom**, which was then headquartered in **Bidar**.

He later became the Prime Minister under the Bahmani rulers, contributing significantly to the administration, military, and educational reforms of the kingdom, including the construction of the famous **Madrasa of Muhammad Gawan** in Bidar.

The options Agra, Delhi, and Fatehpur Sikri are incorrect because they were major centers of the **Mughal Empire**, which was established much later in 1526, long after Muhammad Gawan had already established his influence in the Deccan region.

Therefore, **Bidar** is the historically accurate location associated with his arrival and his subsequent illustrious career in the Bahmani Sultanate.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-25.q: Who was the Contemporary of Louis XIV of France?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-25.explanation:
The correct answer is **Aurangzeb**, who was the contemporary of **Louis XIV**.

Looking at the options provided, there appears to be a mismatch with historical timelines. **Louis XIV** reigned from **1643 to 1715**. Let us evaluate the timeline of the Mughal emperors listed:

* **Babar** reigned from **1526 to 1530**, making him an ancestor of Louis XIV's contemporaries.
* **Akbar** reigned from **1556 to 1605**, preceding the reign of Louis XIV.
* **Jahangir** reigned from **1605 to 1627**, concluding well before Louis XIV ascended the throne.
* **Shah Jahan** reigned from **1628 to 1658**, meaning he was the Mughal emperor during the early years of Louis XIV's reign.

While **Shah Jahan** (Option 3) overlaps with the early years of Louis XIV, the most famous historical contemporary often cited in TNPSC examinations is **Aurangzeb**, who reigned from **1658 to 1707**.

None of the provided options represent the primary contemporary of the "Sun King" throughout his long reign, though **Shah Jahan** is the closest chronologically among the choices. In historical studies, always remember that Louis XIV represents the peak of absolute monarchy in France, corresponding to the late Mughal period in India.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-25.q: Who is the father of Jahangir?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-25.explanation:
The correct answer is **Akbar**.

**Jahangir**, born as **Salim**, was the fourth **Mughal Emperor**. He was the eldest surviving son of **Akbar the Great**.

Here is a quick look at the lineage to clarify the confusion:

1. **Babur** was the founder of the Mughal Empire and the great-grandfather of Jahangir.
2. **Akbar** was the son of Humayun and the father of Jahangir.
3. **Jahangir** succeeded his father, Akbar, to the throne in 1605.
4. **Shah Jahan** was the son of Jahangir, making him the successor to his father, not the father of Jahangir.
5. **Fahien** was a Chinese pilgrim who visited India during the **Gupta period**, long before the Mughal Empire existed.

In summary, **Akbar** is the father of Jahangir, while **Shah Jahan** is the son of Jahangir.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-25.q: Who is the father of Akbar?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-25.explanation:
The correct answer is **Humayun**.

**Akbar**, also known as **Jalal-ud-din Muhammad Akbar**, was the third Mughal emperor. He was born in 1542 at Umarkot to **Humayun** and his wife, **Hamida Banu Begum**.

Here is a quick look at the lineage of the early Mughal emperors:
1. **Babur** was the founder of the Mughal Empire and the grandfather of Akbar.
2. **Humayun** was the son of Babur and the father of Akbar.
3. **Akbar** succeeded his father Humayun to the throne in 1556.

The other options are incorrect for the following reasons:
* **Babur** was Akbar's grandfather, not his father.
* **Shah Jahan** was Akbar's grandson, the son of Jahangir.
* **Guru Tej Bahadur** was the ninth Sikh Guru and a historical contemporary of Aurangzeb, far removed from Akbar's timeline.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-25.q: Who is the father of Babar?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-25.explanation:
The correct answer is **Umar Sheikh Mirza**.

**Babur**, the founder of the **Mughal Empire** in India, was born to **Umar Sheikh Mirza II**. His father was the ruler of **Ferghana**, a small principality in present-day Uzbekistan, and belonged to the **Timurid dynasty**.

Since his father was a direct descendant of the conqueror **Timur** and his mother was a descendant of **Genghis Khan**, Babur inherited a rich legacy of military leadership and royal ambition.

The other options are incorrect because **Guru Shar Roy** is not a historical figure associated with Babur, and **Sher Khan** is a completely different historical figure, better known as **Sher Shah Suri**, who later challenged the Mughal Empire.

Related Facts:
* Babur ascended the throne of Ferghana at the young age of 12.
* His original name was **Zahir-ud-din Muhammad**.
* He successfully established the Mughal Empire after winning the **First Battle of Panipat** in 1526.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-25.q: Who was the Contemporary of Shakespeare?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-25.explanation:
The correct answer is **Akbar**.

William Shakespeare lived from **1564 to 1616**. During this period, the **Mughal Empire** in India was flourishing under the reign of the great emperor **Akbar**, who ruled from **1556 to 1605**.

Here is a breakdown of why the other options do not fit:

* **Babar** was the founder of the Mughal Empire and ruled from **1526 to 1530**, well before Shakespeare's birth.
* **Sher Khan** (Sher Shah Suri) ruled between **1540 and 1545**, which also predates the Elizabethan era.
* **Shah Jahan** ruled from **1628 to 1658**, beginning after Shakespeare had already passed away.

This historical overlap is often noted in **TNPSC history** questions to test your knowledge of global timelines and the synchronization of major world events with Indian history.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-25.q: Who was the Contemporary of Henry IV?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-25.explanation:
The correct answer is **Akbar**. **Henry IV** was the King of France who reigned from 1589 to 1610. During this specific period, the **Mughal Empire** in India was ruled by the Great Emperor **Akbar**, whose reign lasted from 1556 to 1605. Their timelines overlap significantly, making them contemporaries.

Other options are incorrect for the following reasons:
* **Babar** founded the Mughal Empire much earlier, dying in 1530.
* **Shah Jahan** ruled India during the 17th century, primarily from 1628 to 1658, which is after Henry IV's death.
* **Sher Khan**, also known as Sher Shah Suri, ruled during the mid-16th century, well before the reign of Henry IV.

Related Facts:
* Henry IV was the first French monarch of the House of Bourbon.
* Akbar is famous for his policy of religious tolerance, known as Sulh-i-kul.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-25.q: Mahalwari was introduced in which year?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-25.explanation:
The **Mahalwari system** was introduced in **1822**.

This land revenue system was primarily designed by **Holt Mackenzie**. It was implemented in the North-Western Provinces of the Bengal Presidency, which covers large parts of modern-day Uttar Pradesh, parts of Madhya Pradesh, and Punjab.

Under this system:
* The unit of assessment was the **Mahal** (a village or a group of villages).
* The **village headman** or the village community was responsible for collecting and paying the revenue.
* The revenue was not fixed permanently but was subject to periodic revision.

The year 1822 is the correct historical date for the formal introduction of the **Mahalwari Regulation**.

Regarding the other options:
* **1833** is significant for the **Regulation IX of 1833**, which modified the system to make it more practical and less burdensome by simplifying the assessment process.
* **1722** and **1882** are not associated with the primary implementation phases of this specific land revenue policy.

The correct answer is **Abul Fazl**.

**Abul Fazl** was a prominent scholar, philosopher, and the trusted **Vizier** (minister) in the court of the Mughal Emperor **Akbar**. He was one of the **Navaratnas** (nine gems) of Akbar’s royal court.

**Akbarnama** serves as the official chronicle of the reign of Akbar. It is written in **Persian** and provides extensive details regarding the history, administration, and socio-cultural life of the Mughal Empire during that period.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

* **Guru Tegh Bahadur** was the ninth Sikh Guru and is known for his spiritual leadership and martyrdom, not for historical chronicles of the Mughal court.
* **Bairam Khan** was the powerful military commander and guardian of Akbar during his youth, but he was not an author of historical texts.
* **Raja Todar Mal** was Akbar’s **Finance Minister** (Diwan-i-Ashraf), famous for introducing the **Dahshala** land revenue system, rather than writing historical biographies.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-26.q: Who is said to be the guardian of Shivaji?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-26.explanation:
The correct answer is **Dadaji Kondadev**.

**Dadaji Kondadev** was a trusted administrator and advisor appointed by **Shahaji Bhosale**, Shivaji's father, to look after the administration of his *jagir* in Pune.

He played a crucial role in Shivaji's early life by:
* Providing formal training in administration, statecraft, and military tactics.
* Helping Shivaji manage his estate effectively during his formative years.
* Acting as a mentor and guardian while Shivaji's father was stationed in the Deccan/Karnataka region.

**Raja Todar Mal** and **Birbal** were prominent figures in the court of the Mughal Emperor **Akbar**, serving as his finance minister and advisor respectively, and are unrelated to Shivaji's upbringing.

Therefore, **Dadaji Kondadev** is historically recognized as the primary mentor and guardian during Shivaji's childhood.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-26.q: In which year Maratha rule ended?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-26.explanation:
The correct answer is **1853**.

The **Maratha** rule in the region of **Thanjavur** officially came to an end in 1853 following the death of **Shivaji II**. Since he left no direct male heir, the British East India Company applied the **Doctrine of Lapse** to annex the kingdom.

This policy, introduced by **Lord Dalhousie**, allowed the British to seize any princely state where the ruler died without a natural heir.

* The other options (1842, 1832, 1863) are incorrect as they do not mark the annexation of the Thanjavur Maratha state.

Related Facts:
* The Thanjavur Maratha kingdom was established by **Venkoji**, the half-brother of **Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj**.
* The annexation was part of a larger trend of British territorial expansion in 19th-century India.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-26.q: What is the strength of Marathas?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-26.explanation:
The correct answer is **Guerrilla Warfare**, which is historically known as **Ganimi Kava**.

This tactical method was the cornerstone of **Shivaji Maharaj's** military strategy and played a vital role in the rise of the **Maratha Empire**.

Here is why this strategy was so effective:

* **Terrain Advantage**: The Marathas utilized the rugged, hilly landscape of the **Western Ghats** (Sahyadri mountains) to their benefit.
* **Surprise Attacks**: Unlike conventional open-field battles, this approach focused on hit-and-run tactics, ambushes, and rapid movements to exhaust larger, slower-moving enemy armies.
* **Mobility**: By relying on light cavalry and avoiding heavy baggage trains, the Maratha soldiers could strike quickly and disappear before the enemy could organize a counter-offensive.

This strategy allowed them to defeat numerically superior forces, including the massive armies of the **Mughal Empire** and the **Bijapur Sultanate**.

Regarding the other options:

* **Hide and seek warfare** is a colloquial description but is not the formal military term used in history books or competitive exams like the **TNPSC**.
* **Artillery warfare** was actually a significant weakness for the Marathas in their early days, as they struggled to match the heavy cannons used by the Mughals, making this incorrect.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-26.q: What is the Meaning of Sahu?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-26.explanation:
The correct answer is **Honest**.

In the context of the Maratha history and terminology often asked in TNPSC exams, **Sahu** or **Shahu** is derived from the Persian term 'Sah', which signifies a merchant, a gentleman, or a person of high integrity. It represents one who is truthful, trustworthy, and honorable in their dealings.

Other options like 'Obedient', 'Fake', or 'Bad' do not capture the historical and linguistic significance of the term, which is primarily associated with character and social standing.

**Related Facts:**
* **Shahu Maharaj** was a prominent Maratha ruler and the grandson of the great **Shivaji Maharaj**.
* The term 'Sahukar' is often used in Indian society to describe a wealthy and respectable merchant or moneylender.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-26.q: Who is the mughal viceroy of Deccan
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-26.explanation:
The question refers to a historical figure appointed to manage the **Deccan** region during the **Mughal Empire**.

**Prince Murad Bakhsh**, the youngest son of Emperor **Shah Jahan**, was appointed as the Viceroy of the Deccan in 1644. He served in this position for about two years before being replaced by his brother, **Aurangzeb**.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:
* **Prince Antony**, **Prince Adil**, and **Prince Ramdas** are not historical members of the Mughal royal family. These names do not correspond to any known Mughal princes who held the viceroyalty of the Deccan.

The Deccan region was a strategically vital and often rebellious territory for the Mughals. Consequently, it was customary for the Emperors to appoint their own sons or trusted generals to govern the region to maintain firm control.

**Key takeaway:** **Prince Murad** is the only historically accurate figure listed among the options who served as a Mughal Viceroy of the Deccan.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-26.q: Who maintained the records of the king's activities and proceedings in the court?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-26.explanation:
The correct answer is **Waqia-Nawis**.

In the Mughal administrative system, the **Waqia-Nawis** served as the news writer or the official record keeper. They were responsible for documenting the daily activities of the king, the proceedings of the court, and important royal orders.

This role was crucial for the emperor to stay informed about events occurring across his empire. They functioned as the eyes and ears of the administration.

* **Sadar** refers to the head of the religious department.
* **Zampia** is not a standard historical administrative designation in this context.
* **Home Secretary** is a modern administrative title, not applicable to the Mughal era.

Related Facts:
* The **Waqia-Nawis** often reported directly to the central government to ensure transparency.
* They worked alongside the **Sawanih-Nigar**, who provided secret reports to the emperor.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-26.q: The smallest unit with Nine soldiers was headed by whom?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-26.explanation:
In the historical context of the **Maratha military organization** established by **Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj**, the army was structured into specific hierarchical units to ensure discipline and efficiency.

The smallest unit of the infantry consisted of **nine soldiers**. This unit was known as a **Pati** or **Paik**.

The individual in charge of this nine-soldier unit was called a **Naik**.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

* **Havildar**: This rank was higher in the hierarchy and was typically responsible for a larger group of soldiers, usually around fifty.
* **Jamaladar**: This officer held a senior position, commanding a much larger unit of the infantry, often overseeing several smaller units.
* **Home secretary**: This is a modern administrative designation and has no connection to the ancient or medieval military ranking systems of the Maratha era.

Therefore, the **Naik** served as the foundational leader in the infantry hierarchy, directly supervising the smallest squad of nine soldiers.

The correct answer is **Naik**.

In the historical structure of the colonial military organization, specifically within the infantry units, a **Naik** served as a non-commissioned officer who commanded a small group of soldiers. Usually, a group of 5 or more **havildars** or soldiers was placed under the direct supervision of a **Naik** to ensure discipline and tactical order.

Other options are incorrect because:
* **Sadar** refers to the head or chief officer in a department.
* **Jamaladar** is a higher rank in the infantry hierarchy, usually commanding a larger company.
* **Walkia-Nawis** was an official news writer or reporter, not a military commander.

Related Facts:
* The term **Naik** is derived from Sanskrit and implies a leader or guide.
* This rank system was essential for maintaining small-unit cohesion during the period of the East India Company.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-26.q: All public accounts of the kingdom were checked and counter-signed by Whom?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-26.explanation:
The correct answer is **Amatya**. In the **Maratha administration**, the **Amatya** held the significant responsibility of managing the state's finances. He was the chief accountant and finance minister who meticulously checked and counter-signed all public accounts of the kingdom.

* **Sadar** served as the head of religious and ecclesiastical affairs.
* **Wakia-Nawis** acted as the news reporter or chronicler of the court.
* **Naik** usually referred to a local military officer or commander.

Related Facts:
* The **Amatya** was one of the eight ministers known as the **Ashta Pradhan**.
* This council was established by **Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj** to ensure efficient governance.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-26.q: Nadir Shah was assassinated in which year?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-26.explanation:
**Nadir Shah**, the ruler of Persia and the invader who sacked Delhi in 1739, was assassinated in **1747**. He was killed by his own officers while encamped at Fathabad near Khabushan.

The correct year is **1747**.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:
* **1737** was the year he began his campaigns leading up to the invasion of India.
* **1773** and **1787** are dates well after his death, occurring during the period when the **Durrani Empire** was established by his successor, Ahmad Shah Abdali.

Following his death, his vast empire began to disintegrate. This power vacuum allowed **Ahmad Shah Abdali**, one of his most prominent generals, to consolidate power and establish the foundations of modern **Afghanistan**.

questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-27.q: Saraswathi mahal was built by whom?
questions/tm-history-mughals-marathas-27.explanation:
The **Saraswathi Mahal Library** located in **Thanjavur** was primarily developed and enriched by the **Maratha rulers**.
