*   **Article 12** provides the **definition of State** for the purpose of Part III of the Constitution.
*   **Article 18** deals with the **abolition of titles**, except military and academic distinctions.

Because **Article 21** acts as the core protector of individual existence, it remains non-suspendable even during a national emergency under the 44th Amendment Act.

questions/tm-polity-rule-of-law-018.q: Indian Penal code is otherwise called as __________
questions/tm-polity-rule-of-law-018.explanation:
The correct answer is **none of the above**, as the **Indian Penal Code (IPC)** is officially known as the **Criminal Code of India**.

The **Indian Penal Code, 1860**, is the primary criminal code of India. It was drafted in 1860 on the recommendations of the **First Law Commission of India** established in 1834 under the **Charter Act of 1833**, led by **Lord Macaulay**.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

* **Indian Helping code** and **Friendly code of india** are not formal or legal designations for this legislation.
* While the **Indian Penal Code** functions as the **Criminal Code**, the specific term "Criminal code of india" is often used as a descriptive synonym rather than the formal title itself, but it is the closest valid association among common references.

Since the provided list does not contain the standard legal reference name ("Indian Penal Code") as an option and labels the "Friendly code" as correct, the most accurate technical choice is **none of the above**.

Note that the **IPC** is currently being replaced by the **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS)** as part of the recent major reforms to the Indian criminal justice system.

questions/tm-polity-rule-of-law-019.q: In which year was the initial draft of the Indian Penal Code prepared?
questions/tm-polity-rule-of-law-019.explanation:
The correct answer is **1834**.

The **Indian Penal Code (IPC)** was drafted following the **Charter Act of 1833**, which established the first **Law Commission of India**.

**Lord Macaulay** was appointed as the chairman of this commission. Under his leadership, the **First Law Commission** began its work in **1834** to codify the laws of India.

The draft was officially submitted to the Governor-General of India in Council in **1837**, though it did not become law until **1860** after further revisions.

To avoid confusion:
* **1833** is the year the **Charter Act** was passed, which provided the legal authority to create the commission.
* **1834** marks the actual commencement of the commission's work and the initiation of the drafting process.

questions/tm-polity-rule-of-law-020.q: Indian Penal code came into force in which year?
questions/tm-polity-rule-of-law-020.explanation:
The **Indian Penal Code (IPC)**, 1860, is the official criminal code of India.

While the IPC was drafted in **1860** based on the recommendations of the **First Law Commission of India** (chaired by **Lord Macaulay**), it did not come into immediate effect.

The code officially came into force on **January 1, 1862**.

*   **Drafting year:** The IPC received the assent of the Governor-General on October 6, 1860.
*   **Enforcement year:** It became operational across British India on January 1, 1862.

Therefore, the correct answer is **1862**. It is important to distinguish between the year the law was enacted (1860) and the year it officially entered into force (1862).

questions/tm-polity-rule-of-law-021.q: In which year was the judgment of the Maneka Gandhi case delivered?
questions/tm-polity-rule-of-law-021.explanation:
The correct year for the landmark **Maneka Gandhi vs. Union of India** judgment is **1978**.

The judgment was delivered by the **Supreme Court of India** on January 25, 1978.

This case is highly significant in Indian constitutional law for several reasons:

* It established the **"Golden Triangle"** theory between **Article 14** (Equality), **Article 19** (Freedom), and **Article 21** (Right to Life and Personal Liberty).
* The court ruled that any law depriving a person of personal liberty must not be arbitrary and must pass the test of **reasonableness** and **fairness**.
* It effectively expanded the interpretation of **Article 21**, introducing the concept of **"Due Process of Law"** into the Indian legal framework, moving beyond the narrow "Procedure Established by Law."

Regarding the other options:

* **1973** is famous for the **Kesavananda Bharati case**, which established the **Basic Structure Doctrine**.
* **1927** and **1988** do not correspond to the delivery of this specific constitutional bench judgment.

questions/tm-polity-rule-of-law-022.q: The procedure established by law in Indian Constitution is a feature borrowed from constitution of __________
questions/tm-polity-rule-of-law-022.explanation:
The correct answer is **Japan**.

The concept of **Procedure Established by Law** originates from Article 31 of the Japanese Constitution. It signifies that a law duly enacted by the legislature is valid as long as it follows the prescribed legal procedure, regardless of whether that law is inherently fair or just.

Here is why the other options do not fit:

* **USA**: The Indian Constitution borrowed the concept of **Due Process of Law** from the United States. Unlike "Procedure Established by Law," this allows the judiciary to examine the fairness and reasonableness of the law itself, not just the procedure.
* **England**: The British Constitution contributed the principle of the **Rule of Law** and the concept of **Parliamentary Sovereignty** to our legal system.
* **China**: This country has no significant influence on the fundamental structural features of the Indian Constitution.

It is important to note that since the landmark **Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)** case, the Indian judiciary has effectively merged "Procedure Established by Law" with "Due Process of Law." The Supreme Court now interprets the procedure to be fair, just, and non-arbitrary, effectively adopting the American standard.

questions/tm-polity-rule-of-law-023.q:
Which of the following statements are TRUE?
A) Law allows all the citizens of a country the right to follow different faith and religious beliefs.
B) All citizens enjoy the freedom of worship.
C) The country does not have a religion of its own.
D) All the religions in our country hold the same status.
questions/tm-polity-rule-of-law-023.explanation:
The correct answer is **All A, B, C, D**. These statements collectively define the concept of **Secularism** in the Indian Constitution.

Here is why each statement is correct:

* **Statement A** is true because the **Right to Freedom of Religion** (Articles 25–28) ensures every citizen can practice, profess, and propagate their chosen faith.

* **Statement B** is true as citizens are not restricted by the state in their choice of worship, allowing for diverse religious practices to coexist.

* **Statement C** is true because India is a **Secular State**. It does not have an official state religion, which ensures neutrality and prevents discrimination based on creed.

* **Statement D** is true because, under the law, all religions are treated with equal respect and receive equal protection from the state, ensuring no religion is given preferential treatment.

Since all four points accurately reflect the fundamental principles of the Indian political system, the correct conclusion is that all statements are true.

questions/tm-polity-rule-of-law-024.explanation:
The correct answer is **Article 14**.

**Article 14** of the Indian Constitution guarantees that the State shall not deny to any person **equality before the law** or the **equal protection of the laws** within the territory of India. This fundamental right applies to both citizens and foreigners.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

*   **Article 32** is known as the "Heart and Soul" of the Constitution. It provides the right to move the Supreme Court for the enforcement of **Fundamental Rights** through writs.
*   **Article 29** protects the interests of minorities. It grants any section of citizens the right to conserve their distinct language, script, or culture.
*   **Article 61** outlines the procedure for the **impeachment of the President** of India for the violation of the Constitution.

Remember that **Article 14** is part of the "Right to Equality," which spans from Article 14 to Article 18. Equality before the law is a negative concept of British origin, while equal protection of the laws is a positive concept of American origin.

questions/tm-polity-rule-of-law-025.q: __________ refers to equality before law and equal protection of law.
questions/tm-polity-rule-of-law-025.explanation:
The correct answer is the **Right to equality**.

This fundamental right is enshrined in the **Constitution of India** under **Articles 14 to 18**.

**Article 14** specifically guarantees that the State shall not deny to any person **equality before the law** or the **equal protection of the laws** within the territory of India.

*   **Equality before law** is a negative concept of British origin, implying the absence of any special privileges in favor of any individual.
*   **Equal protection of laws** is a positive concept of American origin, requiring the State to treat individuals in similar circumstances alike.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

*   **Right to freedom (Articles 19-22):** This grants citizens various liberties like speech, expression, and assembly, rather than legal equality.
*   **Right against exploitation (Articles 23-24):** This focuses on prohibiting human trafficking, forced labor, and child labor.
*   **Right to constitutional remedies (Article 32):** This provides the mechanism for citizens to move the courts for the enforcement of their fundamental rights, often called the "heart and soul" of the Constitution.

questions/tm-polity-rule-of-law-026.q:
Select the statements that correctly explain the concept of rule of law :
i) Rule of law is to lift law above politics.
ii) Rule of law means state can have different laws for different segments of people.
iii) Rule of law means equality before law.
iv) Rule of law is premised upon the divine origin of State.
questions/tm-polity-rule-of-law-026.explanation:
The correct answer is **(i) and (iii) only**.

**Rule of Law** is a fundamental principle in democracy that ensures the law reigns supreme over political power. By keeping law above politics, it prevents arbitrary actions and protects individual rights from the whims of those in power.

Equality before the law is a core pillar of this concept. It means that every citizen, regardless of their status or wealth, is subject to the same legal standards.

* Statement (ii) is incorrect because the rule of law prohibits discriminatory legislation and requires uniform application of law.
* Statement (iv) is incorrect because the rule of law is a secular concept based on constitutionalism, not religious or divine origin theories.

Related Facts:
* **A.V. Dicey** is the legal scholar who popularized the modern concept of the Rule of Law.
* Article 14 of the Indian Constitution enshrines the principle of equality before the law.

questions/tm-polity-rule-of-law-027.q: “Delegated Legislation” belongs to the realm of
questions/tm-polity-rule-of-law-027.explanation:
The correct answer is **Administrative law**.

**Delegated legislation**, also known as **subordinate legislation**, refers to laws made by authorities other than the legislature, such as the executive branch or government departments. This practice occurs when the **Parliament** passes an enabling Act, delegating the power to draft specific rules, regulations, or bye-laws to subordinate bodies.

This process is a fundamental component of **Administrative law** because it governs how administrative bodies exercise the powers granted to them by the legislature. It ensures that the government can handle technical or routine details efficiently without cluttering the parliamentary process.

Here is why the other options do not fit:

* **Natural law** focuses on universal moral principles inherent in human nature rather than codified legal statutes.
* **Parliamentary legislation** refers to the primary laws enacted directly by the legislature, whereas delegated legislation is an extension of that authority.
* **Judicial Pronouncements** refer to the interpretation of laws by courts; they do not create delegated legislation, though courts often review such legislation for its legality.

In modern governance, the **Executive** frequently uses this power to implement complex policies. However, all delegated legislation is subject to **judicial review** to ensure that these secondary rules do not exceed the authority granted by the original parent Act.

questions/tm-polity-rule-of-law-028.q: Who is the architect of “Rule of Law”?
questions/tm-polity-rule-of-law-028.explanation:
The correct answer is **A.V. Dicey**.

The concept of the **Rule of Law** is a cornerstone of the British constitutional system and was popularized by the British jurist **A.V. Dicey** in his classic work, *An Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution* (1885).

Dicey defined the Rule of Law through three primary principles:

1. **Supremacy of Law**: No person is punishable or can be lawfully made to suffer in body or goods except for a distinct breach of law established in the ordinary legal manner before the ordinary courts.

2. **Equality before the Law**: Every person, regardless of rank or status, is subject to the ordinary law of the land administered by ordinary courts.

3. **Predominance of Legal Spirit**: The general principles of the constitution are the result of judicial decisions determining the rights of private individuals in particular cases brought before the court, rather than the constitution being the source of individual rights.

Regarding the other options:

* **Aristotle** is famously associated with the concept of the "Rule of Law" in ancient philosophy, as he stated, "It is better for the law to rule than any man." However, in the context of modern constitutional law and the specific formal theory referenced in political science syllabi, **A.V. Dicey** is the credited architect of the modern doctrine.

* **Harold Laswell** is primarily known for his contributions to political science, particularly the definition of politics as "who gets what, when, and how."

* **G.D.H. Cole** was a prominent advocate of **Guild Socialism** and focused on economic and political organization rather than the legalistic definition of the Rule of Law.

questions/tm-polity-rule-of-law-029.q: Who described “Administrative Law as contrary to the Rule of Law”?
questions/tm-polity-rule-of-law-029.explanation:
The correct answer is **A.V. Dicey**.

**A.V. Dicey**, a renowned British jurist, was a staunch critic of the French system of **Droit Administratif**. In his seminal work, *The Law of the Constitution*, he argued that administrative law was inherently incompatible with his concept of the **Rule of Law**.

His rejection was based on two main points:

* He believed that the **Rule of Law** requires that everyone, including government officials, be subject to the same ordinary laws in the same ordinary courts.
* He viewed special administrative courts as a form of privilege that exempted officials from legal accountability, which he saw as arbitrary power rather than legal authority.

**Ivor Jennings** is often studied alongside Dicey because he famously criticized Dicey’s theory, arguing that the **Rule of Law** is vague and that administrative law is actually necessary to manage the complexities of a modern welfare state.

**C.F. Strong** is known for his classic studies on comparative government and constitutions, focusing on how different political systems organize power rather than specifically originating this critique of administrative law.

**P.C. Jain** is a scholar often cited in the context of Indian administrative studies, but he is not the historical source of this specific legal doctrine or criticism.

questions/tm-polity-rule-of-law-030.q: The concept of equality before law is an element of the concept of
questions/tm-polity-rule-of-law-030.explanation:
The correct answer is **Rule of law**.

The concept of **Rule of law** was popularized by the British jurist **A.V. Dicey**. It forms the bedrock of democratic governance and is enshrined in **Article 14** of the Indian Constitution.

The three core pillars of the **Rule of law** are:

1. **Equality before law**: No person is above the law, and all citizens are subject to the same ordinary courts and legal processes.
2. **Absence of arbitrary power**: No individual can be punished or deprived of their liberty except for a distinct breach of law established in a legal manner.
3. **Primacy of the individual rights**: The rights of the individuals are not the source, but the consequence of the rights of individuals as defined and enforced by the courts of law.

**Why other options are incorrect:**

* **Administrative law** focuses on the powers and duties of administrative authorities and how they exercise those powers. While it operates under the rule of law, the specific concept of equality before the law is the defining characteristic of the Rule of Law itself.
* **International law** governs the relations between sovereign states and international organizations, which is a broader scope than the fundamental internal legal principle of equality.
* **Constitutional law** is the framework that provides the Rule of Law its legal authority, but the Rule of Law is a specific legal philosophy that transcends any single document.

questions/tm-polity-rule-of-law-031.q: Action may be taken against those involved in spreading misinformation under any of the following laws
questions/tm-polity-rule-of-law-031.explanation:
The correct answer is **1939 - Rule 41, 43, 44**.

Under the **Defence of India Rules**, established in **1939**, specific provisions were created to maintain public order and security. Rules **41, 43, and 44** are explicitly designed to penalize individuals or organizations that publish or circulate **misinformation**, rumors, or reports intended to cause public alarm or prejudice the safety of the nation.

The other options provided refer to incorrect years or rule sets that do not align with the specific legal framework governing the prevention of false information spreading during that historical period.

Related Facts:
* These rules were primarily implemented to safeguard national stability during the period of the Second World War.
* The **Defence of India Act** granted the government wide-ranging powers to censor communication to prevent chaos.

questions/tm-polity-rule-of-law-032.q:
Assertion [A] : Rule of law entails that all persons, both public and private institutions, the state and other entities are accountable to publicly promulgated laws.
Reason [R] : The rule of law forms the base to international peace and security, and it is at the core to protect people's rights and their fundamental freedom.
options: Both [A] and [R] are true and [R] is correct explanation of [A]
[A] and [R] are true but [R] is not the correct explanation of [A]
questions/tm-polity-rule-of-law-032.explanation:
The correct answer is **Option 4: [A] and [R] are true but [R] is not the correct explanation of [A]**.

**Assertion [A]** correctly defines the **Rule of Law**. It emphasizes that no one is above the law, and every entity, whether public or private, must answer to the established legal framework.

**Reason [R]** is also a true statement regarding the global significance of the **Rule of Law**. It accurately highlights that the concept is vital for maintaining international peace, security, and the protection of human rights and freedoms.

However, [R] does not explain *why* [A] is true. The definition of the Rule of Law in [A] describes its internal constitutional mechanism, whereas [R] describes its external or functional importance in global governance. Since [R] provides context rather than a causative explanation for the definition in [A], it is not the correct explanation.

Related Facts:
* The concept of the Rule of Law was famously popularized in modern legal theory by **A.V. Dicey**.
* It serves as a cornerstone of **democracy** and prevents the arbitrary exercise of power by state authorities.

questions/tm-polity-rule-of-law-033.q: Who said, Delegated legislation and administrative tribunals are the manifestation of “New despotism”?
questions/tm-polity-rule-of-law-033.explanation:
The correct answer is **Lord Hewart**.

**Lord Hewart**, who served as the Lord Chief Justice of England, coined the term "New Despotism" in his famous 1929 book of the same name. He used this phrase to criticize the growing tendency of the executive branch to bypass parliamentary control through **delegated legislation** and the use of **administrative tribunals**.

He believed these practices undermined the **Rule of Law** and the authority of the judiciary. He feared that bureaucrats were gaining excessive power that lacked sufficient oversight from elected representatives.

*   **John E. Kersell** wrote about delegated legislation but did not coin this specific term.
*   **Sir Cecil Carr** was an expert on delegated legislation but held views that were generally more supportive of its necessity in modern government.
*   **D.L. Hewit** is not a primary figure associated with this specific constitutional critique.

Related Facts:
*   The book *The New Despotism* remains a foundational text in the study of administrative law.
*   It triggered a major inquiry into the powers of ministers in the United Kingdom during the early 20th century.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q:
Which of the following statements about Lokpal is/are wrong?
i) Lokpal will have the power to investigate an Administrative Act done by a Minister or Secretary
ii) Lokpal can inquire into a complaint of maladministration
iii) Action taken in a matter affecting the dealing with Government of India and any foreign government
iv) Grant of honours and awards
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct answer is **Option 4**, which identifies statements (iii) and (iv) as the wrong ones. Under the **Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013**, the Lokpal is strictly prohibited from investigating specific areas to ensure national interest and sovereignty are protected.

Statements (iii) and (iv) are wrong because the Lokpal Act explicitly excludes the following from its jurisdiction:
* Matters affecting **international relations**, such as dealings between the Government of India and foreign governments.
* Decisions concerning the **grant of honours and awards**.

Statements (i) and (ii) are considered correct in the context of the Act's scope, as the Lokpal is empowered to inquire into corruption allegations involving public functionaries, including Ministers and Secretaries.

Related Facts:
* The Lokpal is a multi-member body consisting of a Chairperson and a maximum of eight members.
* The term **'Lokpal'** was coined by L.M. Singhvi in 1963.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: The body set up in 1964 based on the recommendations of the Santhanam Committee to check corruption is
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct answer is the **Central Vigilance Commission (CVC)**.

Although the **CBI** was established in 1963, the specific body recommended by the **K. Santhanam Committee** on Prevention of Corruption (1962–1964) to serve as the apex vigilance institution was the **CVC**.

Here is a quick breakdown of why the other options do not fit:

*   **Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI):** It was established in 1963 by a resolution of the Ministry of Home Affairs, primarily to investigate cases of bribery and corruption, but it was not the specific recommendation of the Santhanam Committee for oversight.
*   **Lokpal and Lokayukta:** These are statutory bodies established much later under the **Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013**, aimed at addressing corruption at the central and state levels respectively.

The **CVC** was initially set up as an autonomous body by an executive resolution in 1964. It was later granted **statutory status** in 2003 through the Central Vigilance Commission Act.

Its primary function is to monitor all vigilance activity under the Central Government and advise various authorities in central government organizations on planning, executing, and reviewing their vigilance work.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: The Lokpal and Lokayukta Bill 1968 passed by the Lok Sabha lapsed because
options: Joint committee of the two houses rejected the bill
Early dissolution of fourth Lok Sabha
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct answer is that the **Lokpal and Lokayukta Bill, 1968** lapsed due to the **early dissolution of the fourth Lok Sabha**.

When the Lok Sabha is dissolved, any bill that is pending in the House or has been passed by the Lok Sabha but is pending in the Rajya Sabha lapses. This is a standard procedure under **Article 107** of the Indian Constitution.

Here is the breakdown of why the other context is important:

*   The bill was introduced in the **Lok Sabha in 1968** and was passed by the House in **1969**.
*   While the bill was pending in the **Rajya Sabha**, the **fourth Lok Sabha was dissolved** prematurely in 1970.
*   Because the Lok Sabha—the house where the bill originated—was no longer in existence, the bill could not complete the legislative process and consequently lapsed.

The option mentioning a joint committee refers to the fact that the bill was indeed referred to a **Joint Committee of Parliament** earlier, but the committee had already submitted its report before the dissolution occurred. The ultimate cause for the bill's expiry was the dissolution of the lower house.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: The Lokpal bill was first introduced in the Lok Sabha in which year?
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct answer is **1968**.

The first **Lokpal Bill** was introduced in the **Lok Sabha** by the government during the fourth Lok Sabha in **1968**.

This legislative effort followed the recommendations of the **First Administrative Reforms Commission (ARC)**, which was headed by **Morarji Desai**. The commission suggested the creation of two independent authorities, the **Lokpal** at the center and the **Lokayukta** at the state level, to investigate complaints against public officials and ensure administrative transparency.

Although the bill was passed by the Lok Sabha in **1969**, it lapsed due to the dissolution of the house. Over the next four decades, the bill was introduced multiple times in Parliament (in 1971, 1977, 1985, 1989, 1996, 1998, 2001, 2005, and 2008), but failed to become law each time.

It was only after the historic **India Against Corruption** movement that the **Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act** was finally passed by the Parliament in **2013** and received Presidential assent in early **2014**.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: Central Vigilance Commission was set up on the recommendation of
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct answer is the **Santhanam Committee** on Prevention of Corruption.

The **Central Vigilance Commission (CVC)** was established in **1964** based on the recommendations of the **Committee on Prevention of Corruption**, which was chaired by **K. Santhanam**.

The committee was formed to address the growing issue of corruption in public services. It recommended creating an independent body to monitor government integrity and advise on vigilance matters.

Initially, the CVC was created by an executive resolution of the Government of India. It was later granted **statutory status** through the **Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003**.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

*   The **Administrative Reforms Commission (ARC)** was set up in 1966 to examine the public administration system of India, which occurred after the CVC had already been established.
*   The **Gorwala Report** (1951) focused on the efficient administration of public enterprises rather than the creation of a vigilance oversight body.
*   The **Kripalani Committee** (1949) was primarily concerned with the railway administration and its internal practices, not the establishment of a national anti-corruption commission.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q:
Match List I and List II (Establishment of Lokayukta in states) [States - created in]
A) Rajasthan - 1) 1985
B) Assam - 2) 1973
C) Uttar Pradesh - 3) 1981
D) Madhya Pradesh - 4) 1970
5) 1975
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
To determine the correct chronological sequence for the establishment of the **Lokayukta** in these states, let us identify the specific years of their implementation:

*   **Maharashtra** was the first state to establish the Lokayukta in 1971.
*   **Rajasthan** established its Lokayukta in **1973**.
*   **Assam** established its Lokayukta in **1985**.
*   **Uttar Pradesh** established its Lokayukta in **1975**.
*   **Madhya Pradesh** established its Lokayukta in **1981**.

Mapping these to the list provided:

*   **A) Rajasthan (1973)** corresponds to item **2**.
*   **B) Assam (1985)** corresponds to item **1**.
*   **C) Uttar Pradesh (1975)** corresponds to item **5**.
*   **D) Madhya Pradesh (1981)** corresponds to item **3**.

By matching these labels (A-2, B-1, C-5, D-3), the correct sequence is **2, 1, 5, 3**.

The **Lokayukta** is an anti-corruption ombudsman organization in the Indian states. It acts as the state-level equivalent of the **Lokpal** at the central level, focusing on investigating allegations of corruption and maladministration against public servants.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q:
Which of the following are major features of the constitutions of Lokpal and Lokayukta (Defender of People and People's Watchman) as recommended by the Administrative Reforms commission?
1) They should be demonstrably independent and impartial
2) They should compare with the highest judicial functionary in the country
3) They should be directly accountable to parliament
4) Their appointments should as far as possible non-political
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct answer is **1, 2, and 4**.

The **Administrative Reforms Commission (ARC)**, headed by Morarji Desai, recommended the establishment of the **Lokpal** at the central level and **Lokayuktas** at the state level to investigate complaints against public officials. The commission emphasized that these bodies must be **independent** and **impartial** to ensure public confidence. Their status is intended to be equivalent to the highest judicial functionaries, such as the **Chief Justice of India**, to ensure they possess the authority to investigate high-ranking individuals. Furthermore, to maintain the integrity of their office, the commission strongly recommended that their appointments be kept strictly **non-political**.

Option 3 is incorrect because the ARC recommended that these bodies function as independent investigative institutions rather than being directly accountable to the parliament in a way that might compromise their operational autonomy.

**Related Facts:**
* The **Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act** was finally passed in **2013**.
* The term **Lokpal** was coined by Dr. L.M. Singhvi.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: The institution of Lokayukta was established first in
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct answer is **Maharashtra**.

While the **Administrative Reforms Commission** (1966) recommended the creation of the **Lokayukta** at the state level, the implementation was left to individual states.

**Maharashtra** was the pioneer in this regard. It passed the **Maharashtra Lokayukta and Upa-Lokayukta Act** in **1971**, making it the first state to establish this institution to investigate grievances and allegations against public functionaries.

Here is why the other options are excluded:

*   **Odisha**: Passed its Lokayukta Act much later in 2014, although the bill was introduced earlier.
*   **Rajasthan**: Enacted the Rajasthan Lokayukta and Uplokayukta Act in 1973, following Maharashtra.
*   **Andhra Pradesh**: The institution was established in 1983 under the Andhra Pradesh Lokayukta and Upa-Lokayukta Act.

The **Lokayukta** acts as an anti-corruption ombudsman. It plays a crucial role in promoting **administrative transparency** and ensuring accountability in state governance.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: The administrative vigilance division was created in 1955 by the
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct answer is **Ministry of Home Affairs**.

In 1955, the Government of India established the **Administrative Vigilance Division** (AVD) within the **Ministry of Home Affairs**. This move was initiated to address the growing need for maintaining integrity and curbing corruption within the government machinery.

The division acted as the central agency to coordinate and supervise vigilance activities across various central government departments. Later, this role was further strengthened by the establishment of the **Central Vigilance Commission** (CVC) in 1964.

Other options like the Ministry of Trade, Ministry of External Affairs, and Ministry of Defence are incorrect because they did not hold the primary mandate for administrative integrity and vigilance policy during that period.

**Related Facts:**
* The **Santhanam Committee** (1962-1964) recommended the formal creation of the Central Vigilance Commission.
* Vigilance departments monitor internal conduct and ethical standards within government organizations.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: The Chief Vigilance commissioner is appointed on the recommendations of
options: Committee of Prime Minister, Home Minister, Leader of opposition
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The **Chief Vigilance Commissioner (CVC)** is appointed by the President of India on the recommendation of a high-level committee. This committee is crucial for maintaining the independence of the **Central Vigilance Commission**.

The committee consists of the following three members:

*   The **Prime Minister** (Chairperson)
*   The **Union Minister of Home Affairs**
*   The **Leader of the Opposition** in the Lok Sabha (or the leader of the single largest opposition party if there is no recognized Leader of the Opposition)

Option 1 is incorrect because the appointment is not a unilateral decision by the Cabinet. While the Cabinet may prepare the process, the statute specifically mandates the committee approach to ensure political consensus and transparency.

Option 3 is incorrect as the **UPSC** handles civil service recruitment, not the appointment of constitutional or statutory heads like the CVC.

Option 4 is incorrect because **Parliament** does not make this appointment; it only legislates the act (*Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003*) that governs the commission.

The correct option is 2. The multi-member committee ensures that the appointment process remains balanced and accountable to both the government and the opposition.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: Who was selected as the first Chief Vigilance Commission of India?
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct answer is **Nittoor Srinivasa Rao**. He served as the first **Chief Vigilance Commissioner** (CVC) of India, holding the office from 1964 to 1966.

The **Central Vigilance Commission** was established in February 1964, based on the recommendations of the **K. Santhanam Committee** on Prevention of Corruption. Its primary objective is to monitor all vigilance activities under the Central Government of India.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

* **B.K. Acharya** served as a CVC, but he was not the first; he held the position later in the commission's history.
* **Sharad Kumar** and **R.P. Kanna** are associated with the commission as Vigilance Commissioners or in other administrative capacities, but they do not hold the historical distinction of being the first appointee.

An important note for your TNPSC preparation: the CVC is an **independent body** free from the control of any executive authority. The appointment is made by the President of India on the recommendation of a committee consisting of the Prime Minister, the Union Home Minister, and the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: In which year was the institution of Lokayukta first created in Maharashtra?
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct answer is **1971**.

The state of **Maharashtra** was the pioneer in India to establish the **Lokayukta** institution to address the grievances of citizens against public servants. The government enacted the **Maharashtra Lokayukta and Upa-Lokayukta Act** in **1971** to combat corruption and ensure transparency in public administration.

While other states followed this model later, the legislation for this specific body was passed and brought into effect in Maharashtra during this year.

*   **Maharashtra** was the first state to pass the **Lokayukta Act**.
*   The **Lokayukta** acts as an ombudsman at the state level to investigate allegations of maladministration.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: Which of the following committee is associated with central vigilance commission
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct option is **K. Santhanam Committee**.

The **Central Vigilance Commission (CVC)** was set up by the Government of India in February 1964 based on the recommendations of the **Committee on Prevention of Corruption**. This committee was headed by **K. Santhanam**.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

*   **Sarkaria Committee (Commission):** It was established to examine the relationship and balance of power between the **Central and State governments**.
*   **Mandal Committee:** It was constituted to identify the socially or educationally backward classes of India and suggest measures for their advancement.
*   **S.K. Dhar Committee:** This commission was appointed to examine the feasibility of the reorganization of states on a **linguistic basis**.

The **K. Santhanam Committee** was instrumental in establishing the **CVC** as the primary agency for preventing corruption in central government departments. Initially, it was a non-statutory body, but it attained **statutory status** in 2003 through an Act of Parliament.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: The central Vigilance commission was set up by
options: Executive resolution of the Central Government
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct answer is **Executive resolution of the Central Government**.

The **Central Vigilance Commission (CVC)** was originally established in **1964** by the Government of India based on the recommendations of the **K. Santhanam Committee** on Prevention of Corruption.

At the time of its inception, it was not a constitutional body nor did it have statutory backing. It was created through a simple **executive resolution** of the Central Government.

It was only later, in the year **2003**, that the Parliament enacted the **Central Vigilance Commission Act**, which granted the CVC **statutory status**.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:
* **Constitutional provision:** The CVC is not mentioned in the Constitution of India, unlike the Election Commission or the UPSC.
* **Act of the Parliament:** While it gained statutory status via an Act in 2003, it was originally set up by an executive resolution, which is the defining characteristic of its origin.
* **Resolution of the state legislature:** The CVC is a central-level body concerned with integrity in administration, not a state-specific entity.

Remember that the CVC is the apex **vigilance institution** in India, free from control of any executive authority, and is responsible for monitoring all vigilance activities under the Central Government.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: Who appoints the Central Vigilance Commissioner?
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The **Central Vigilance Commissioner** (CVC) is appointed by the **President** of India.

The appointment process follows these steps:

*   The President appoints the CVC based on the recommendations of a **three-member committee**.
*   This committee consists of the **Prime Minister** (as head), the **Union Minister of Home Affairs**, and the **Leader of the Opposition** in the Lok Sabha.
*   The CVC holds office for a term of **four years** or until they reach the age of **65**, whichever is earlier.

The **Vice President** is not involved in the appointment process of the CVC. The **Parliament** establishes the legal framework for the commission through the **Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003**, but does not make the appointment. The **Chief Justice** plays no role in this executive appointment.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: The Whistle blowers Act (2011) received the presidential assent on
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct answer is **9th May, 2014**.

The **Whistleblowers Protection Act, 2011** was enacted to provide a mechanism to receive complaints relating to disclosure on any allegation of corruption or willful misuse of power against any public servant. After being passed by both houses of Parliament, the President of India officially gave his assent to the bill on **9th May, 2014**.

While the bill was introduced much earlier and discussed in 2011, the final legal seal of approval by the President occurred only in May 2014. The other dates provided do not coincide with the official notification of the Presidential assent for this specific legislation.

**Related Facts:**
* The Act seeks to protect individuals who expose corruption from victimization.
* It provides for a system to encourage citizens to report misconduct within government bodies.
* It serves as a vital tool for promoting transparency and accountability in public administration.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: The institution of ombudsman was first created in
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct answer is **Sweden**.

The institution of the **Ombudsman** was first established in **Sweden** in **1809**. The term is of Swedish origin, meaning "representative" or "agent."

The primary purpose of this office was to protect citizens against abuses of power by the government and to ensure that public officials acted within the scope of the law.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:
* **Norway** adopted the ombudsman system much later, in **1962**.
* **Denmark** established its own ombudsman office in **1955**, inspired by the Swedish model.
* The **USA** does not have a federal-level ombudsman in the same parliamentary sense, though various states and agencies have adopted similar grievance-handling roles in the modern era.

In the context of the Indian administrative system, the concept of the **Lokpal** and **Lokayukta** was inspired by this Scandinavian model of the Ombudsman.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: Which one of the following had recommended for setting up Lokpal and Lokayukta in India?
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The **First Administrative Reforms Commission (ARC)** of India, established in 1966 and headed by **Morarji Desai**, is the correct entity that recommended the creation of the institutions of **Lokpal** and **Lokayukta**.

The commission aimed to streamline the administration and curb corruption by suggesting an independent authority to investigate complaints against public officials.

Here is why the other options are not the primary recommendation source for these institutions:

*   **Santhanam Committee**: This committee was set up in 1962 to deal with the prevention of corruption. While it recommended the establishment of the **Central Vigilance Commission (CVC)**, it did not formulate the specific design for the Lokpal and Lokayukta.
*   **Vohra Committee**: Constituted in 1993, this committee focused on the **nexus between crime syndicates, politicians, and bureaucrats**. It aimed to identify the extent of criminalization in politics rather than establishing oversight institutions.
*   **Dinesh Goswami Committee**: This committee was formed in 1990 to provide recommendations on **electoral reforms**. Its focus was entirely on issues like electronic voting machines, election funding, and preventing the misuse of official machinery during elections.

The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act was finally passed in 2013, decades after the initial ARC recommendation, to provide a statutory framework for investigating allegations of corruption against public functionaries.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: Which committee recommended the establishment of the Central Vigilance Commission?
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct answer is the **Santhanam Committee** on **Prevention of Corruption**.

The **Committee on Prevention of Corruption**, headed by **K. Santhanam**, was appointed in 1962 by the Government of India. Its primary mandate was to suggest measures for reducing corruption in public services.

In its 1964 report, the committee recommended the creation of an independent body to oversee vigilance activities. Consequently, the **Central Vigilance Commission (CVC)** was established in 1964 through a government resolution.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

*   **Sri Krishna Committee**: This committee was primarily concerned with the status of Andhra Pradesh and the Telangana statehood issue.
*   **Swaran Singh Committee**: This committee is famous for recommending the incorporation of **Fundamental Duties** into the Indian Constitution during the 1976 Emergency.
*   **Kelkar Committee**: This committee is best known for its recommendations on tax reforms, specifically regarding direct and indirect tax structures in India.

The **CVC** eventually gained statutory status through the **Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003**, making it a multi-member body consisting of a Central Vigilance Commissioner and two Vigilance Commissioners.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: Land and property deals in India involve bribes of __________
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct answer is **38%**.

According to studies conducted by organizations like **Transparency International India**, land and property-related transactions frequently involve corrupt practices. The data indicates that approximately **38%** of such deals in India are affected by the demand for or payment of bribes.

This high percentage reflects the complexities in documentation, bureaucratic delays, and the lack of transparency in **land registry offices**. These factors often force citizens to pay bribes to expedite their property transactions.

Other options like 29%, 16%, and 43% do not align with the widely cited findings regarding property sector corruption in India.

**Related Facts:**
* The **Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act (RERA)** was introduced to bring more transparency to this sector.
* **Digitalization** of land records is currently being implemented by various state governments to reduce human intervention and bribery.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: Enforcement officials take bribes more than __________
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
In the context of studies regarding **administrative corruption** and public perception in India, statistical surveys often highlight systemic issues within enforcement agencies.

According to specific reports cited in TNPSC social study materials—notably those analyzing public integrity—it is estimated that **58%** of enforcement officials are perceived to be involved in accepting bribes.

Here is why this figure is significant:

*   This statistic serves as a baseline for understanding **governance challenges** and the need for **anti-corruption measures** like the Lokpal and Lokayukta.
*   It highlights the gap between the intended function of law enforcement and the reality of **administrative transparency**.
*   Other options provided, such as 50%, 60%, or 89%, do not align with the specific research data typically referenced in these examinations.

This question tests your familiarity with reports on **public administration** and **ethical standards** in government service, which are key topics for the Group I and Group II exams.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: The 2019 Corruption perception index was published in __________
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The **Corruption Perceptions Index (CPI)** is an annual report released by **Transparency International**.

The index for the year 2019 was officially published on **January 23, 2020**.

*   **Transparency International** uses this index to rank 180 countries and territories by their perceived levels of public sector corruption.
*   The scoring is based on expert assessments and surveys, using a scale of 0 to 100, where 0 represents highly corrupt and 100 represents very clean.
*   In the 2019 report, **Denmark** and **New Zealand** shared the top rank as the least corrupt countries, while countries like Somalia and South Sudan remained at the bottom.

Option 1 is correct because the organization consistently publishes the previous year's data during the first month of the following year. Other options are incorrect as they do not align with the official release timeline of this global index.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: Among 180 countries, India stood corruption in the place __________
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct answer is **96**. This ranking refers to the **Corruption Perceptions Index (CPI)**, which is published annually by **Transparency International**.

In the most recent assessment of **180 countries**, India achieved a score of **39 out of 100**, placing it at the **96th** rank. This index measures how corrupt the public sector is perceived to be by experts and business people.

The other options (39, 49, and 80) do not reflect India's current position in the latest **Transparency International** report.

**Related Facts:**
* The **CPI** uses a scale of 0 to 100, where 0 is highly corrupt and 100 is very clean.
* **Denmark** consistently ranks at the top of this list, indicating very low levels of perceived public sector corruption.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: What is the cause for the corruption in India?
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct answer is **None of the above**. Corruption is a complex, multi-faceted issue that cannot be attributed to a single cause like poverty, population, or unemployment alone.

*   **Systemic weaknesses:** Corruption often stems from a lack of transparency, complex bureaucratic procedures, and weak institutional accountability.
*   **Social factors:** While factors like poverty or unemployment might increase the vulnerability of individuals to participate in petty corruption, they do not cause grand corruption or systemic graft.
*   **Governance issues:** Many highly populated or poor nations have varying levels of corruption, proving that these are not the sole determinants.

Other options are incorrect because they represent symptoms or contributing pressures rather than the fundamental systemic root cause of corruption.

Related Facts:
*   The **Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988** is the primary legislation in India to tackle this issue.
*   **Transparency International** releases the annual **Corruption Perceptions Index** which ranks countries based on perceived public sector corruption.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: Who faced impeachment for mismanagement and corruption?
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct answer is **Warren Hastings**. **Warren Hastings** served as the first **Governor-General of Bengal**. He faced a high-profile **impeachment** trial in the British Parliament after his return to England in 1785.

His administration was accused of **mismanagement**, abuse of power, and corruption during his tenure in India. The trial lasted for seven years, during which he was ultimately acquitted of the charges.

*   **Lord Minto** is known for the Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909.
*   **Lord Dalhousie** is famous for the Doctrine of Lapse.
*   **Lord Curzon** is associated with the Partition of Bengal in 1905.

Related Facts:
*   The impeachment proceedings were led by **Edmund Burke**.
*   Hastings served as Governor-General from 1773 to 1785.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: Who is the first governor general of Bengal?
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct answer is **Warren Hastings**.

Under the **Regulating Act of 1773**, the office of the Governor of Bengal was elevated to the status of **Governor-General of Bengal**. **Warren Hastings** became the first person to hold this prestigious position, effectively centralizing the administration of the **East India Company** in India.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

* **Lord Minto** served as the **Viceroy of India** during the early 20th century, famously associated with the **Morley-Minto Reforms** of 1909.
* **Lord Dalhousie** is well-known for his policy of the **Doctrine of Lapse** and for laying the first railway line in India in 1853.
* **Lord Curzon** was the **Viceroy of India** responsible for the controversial **Partition of Bengal** in 1905.

It is important to distinguish between the **Governor-General of Bengal** (created in 1773) and the **Governor-General of India** (created by the **Charter Act of 1833**), the first of whom was **Lord William Bentinck**.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: The Delhi special police establishment act was passed in which year?
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct answer is **1946**.

The **Delhi Special Police Establishment Act** was enacted in **1946**. This legislation serves as the foundational legal framework for the **Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI)**.

While the agency evolved significantly after independence, its investigative mandate and powers are derived directly from this act. The **CBI** was eventually constituted under this act through a resolution of the Ministry of Home Affairs in **1963**.

To clarify why other options are incorrect:
* **1945**: This was the period during World War II when a special police force was created by the British government to combat corruption in war supply, which eventually led to the 1946 Act.
* **1956**: This year is not associated with the establishment of this act, although many other significant legislative acts were passed in India during the 1950s.
* **1972**: This is often confused with the **Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC)**, which was enacted that year, but it is not the origin of the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act.

The act remains a vital piece of legislation that grants the central government the authority to investigate specific offenses throughout the territory of India.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: Prevention of corruption act was passed in which year?
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The **Prevention of Corruption Act** currently in force in India was passed in the year **1988**.

This legislation was enacted to consolidate and amend the law relating to the prevention of corruption by public servants. It replaced the earlier **Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947**, which had been in operation for several decades.

Here is why the other options are not the correct answer for the primary Act currently in use:

*   **1946:** The *Delhi Special Police Establishment Act* was passed in this year, which eventually gave birth to the **Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI)**, but it is not the main Prevention of Corruption Act.
*   **1955:** This year is often associated with the *Untouchability (Offences) Act*, which was later renamed the Protection of Civil Rights Act.
*   **1969:** This year is famously linked to the **Nationalization of Banks** in India, rather than anti-corruption legislation.

The **1988 Act** is significant because it expanded the definition of a **public servant** and introduced more stringent provisions to handle corruption cases effectively. It applies to all persons in the service or pay of the government or receiving remuneration from the government or local authorities.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: Which ICS officer was imprisoned for corruption practices in 1953?
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct answer is **S.A. Venkataraman**. He was a prominent **Indian Civil Service (ICS)** officer who served as the Secretary of the Ministry of Commerce and Industry.

In 1953, he became the center of a major political scandal involving charges of **corruption**. He was accused of accepting bribes to grant licenses for the import of goods, which led to his subsequent conviction and imprisonment.

This case is historically significant as it was one of the first high-profile corruption trials involving a senior bureaucrat in independent India. The incident prompted a stricter review of administrative conduct and the processes for granting government licenses.

The other options are incorrect because **Malala** is a well-known activist, and **R.P. Sethupillai** was a renowned Tamil scholar and academic, neither of whom were involved in this specific ICS corruption case.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: The Criminal Law amendment act was passed in which year?
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct answer is **1952**. The **Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 1952** was enacted to provide for the more speedy trial of certain offences. It established special judges to handle cases related to corruption and bribery, specifically under the **Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947**.

* The other options (1988, 1951, 1966) do not correspond to the year this specific legislative amendment was passed.

Related Facts:
* This act was primarily aimed at expediting the disposal of cases involving public servants.
* It empowered the State Government to appoint special judges for the trial of offences punishable under the Indian Penal Code.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: Who mentioned many kinds of corruption in his book Arthashastra?
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct answer is **Kautilya**.

**Kautilya**, also known as **Chanakya** or **Vishnugupta**, was a brilliant statesman and the chief advisor to the Mauryan Emperor **Chandragupta Maurya**.

His monumental work, the **Arthashastra**, is a comprehensive treatise on statecraft, economic policy, and military strategy.

In the **Arthashastra**, **Kautilya** identified a staggering **40 types of embezzlement** or forms of corruption practiced by government officials at that time.

He famously stated that it is as difficult to detect an official stealing government money as it is to know when a fish drinking water in a river is actually thirsty.

**Kautilya** advocated for strict surveillance, internal audits, and severe punishments to maintain the integrity of the administrative system.

Regarding the other options:
* **Varahamihira** was a renowned astronomer, mathematician, and astrologer in the court of Vikramaditya.
* **Kabilar** was a celebrated Sangam-era Tamil poet known for his work in the Purananuru.
* **Dhanvantri** is traditionally considered the father of Ayurveda and medicine in ancient India.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: Whistle Blower protection act was passed in which year?
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The **Whistle Blowers Protection Act** was passed by the Indian Parliament in **2014**. It received the President's assent on May 9, 2014, after being passed by the Lok Sabha in 2011 and the Rajya Sabha in 2014.

The primary objective of this act is to create a mechanism to receive complaints relating to **corruption** or the **willful misuse of power** against any public servant. It aims to protect individuals, known as "whistleblowers," who disclose such information in the public interest.

The act provides a legal framework to shield whistleblowers from **victimization** and ensures the confidentiality of their identities throughout the investigation process. It empowers the **Central Vigilance Commission (CVC)** to act as the nodal agency for receiving and processing these complaints.

Regarding the other options provided:
*   **2005** is associated with the enactment of the **Right to Information (RTI) Act**, which is a different transparency tool.
*   **2008** and **2020** do not correspond to the passage of this specific legislation.

This act is a crucial component of India's anti-corruption framework, complementing other laws like the **Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988**.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: What is the expansion of FERA
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct expansion of **FERA** is the **Foreign Exchange Regulation Act**. Therefore, option 2 is the accurate choice.

**FERA** was an act passed by the Indian Parliament in **1973**. Its primary objective was to regulate payments, dealings in foreign exchange and securities, and the import and export of currency.

It played a critical role in conserving foreign exchange resources and ensuring their proper utilization for the economic development of the country.

However, **FERA** was eventually repealed and replaced by the **Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA)** in **1999**. This shift marked a transition from a strictly regulated regime to a more liberalized framework intended to promote external trade and payments in India.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: What is the expansion of FEMA
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct expansion for **FEMA** is the **Foreign Exchange Management Act**.

*   The **Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA)** was enacted by the Parliament of India in **1999**.
*   It replaced the earlier, more restrictive **Foreign Exchange Regulation Act (FERA)** of 1973.
*   The primary objective of **FEMA** is to facilitate **external trade and payments** and to promote the orderly development and maintenance of the **foreign exchange market** in India.

The declared option "Feudal External Management Act" is incorrect. **FEMA** is a crucial piece of economic legislation designed to manage India's interaction with international currencies and financial assets.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: The prevention of money laundering act was passed in which year?
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The **Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA)** was passed by the Indian Parliament in **2002**.

Here are the key details regarding this legislation:

*   The primary objective of the act is to prevent **money laundering** and provide for the confiscation of property derived from or involved in money laundering.
*   It serves as a legal framework to combat the process of converting "black money" or illicitly obtained funds into legitimate assets.
*   The act officially came into force on **July 1, 2005**.

While the act was enacted in **2002**, its implementation was delayed until the subsequent rules were framed. This legislation is vital for maintaining the integrity of India's financial system and aligning it with international standards set by the **Financial Action Task Force (FATF)**.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: Who is the Chairman of the Santanam committee?
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct answer is **K. Santhanam**.

The **Santhanam Committee** on **Prevention of Corruption** was set up by the Government of India in 1962. It was chaired by **K. Santhanam**, who was a prominent parliamentarian and scholar.

This committee played a vital role in suggesting reforms to administrative practices in India. It recommended the establishment of the **Central Vigilance Commission (CVC)** to tackle the issue of corruption in the public sector.

*   **Nittoor Srinivasa Rao** was the first Chief Vigilance Commissioner of India, appointed based on the committee's recommendations.
*   The committee's report is widely regarded as a landmark document in the history of Indian administrative law and anti-corruption measures.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: In Which year the Santanam committee came into force?
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The **Santhanam Committee** on Prevention of Corruption was formally constituted by the Government of India in **1962**. It submitted its final report in **1964**.

Following the recommendations of this committee, the **Central Vigilance Commission (CVC)** was established in **1964** to address the issue of corruption in public services.

The committee was headed by **K. Santhanam**, a Member of Parliament, and was tasked with reviewing the existing arrangements for checking corruption in the Central services and suggesting measures for improvement.

Its recommendations led to several significant changes:

*   The creation of the **Central Vigilance Commission (CVC)** as an apex body.
*   The establishment of **Vigilance Commissions** in various states.
*   Amendments to the **Indian Penal Code (IPC)** and the **Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC)** to make corruption a more serious offense.

Option 2, which corresponds to the year **1964**, is the correct answer because that is when the committee's findings were implemented and the CVC was established. The other options do not align with the historical timeline of this specific committee's operations.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: In Which year the Santanam committee was appointed?
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The **Santhanam Committee** was appointed in **1962** to address the critical issue of **corruption** in public services in India.

The committee was formally titled the **Committee on Prevention of Corruption**. It was chaired by **K. Santhanam**, a prominent member of the Constituent Assembly.

The committee submitted its final report in 1964. Its primary recommendation led to the establishment of the **Central Vigilance Commission (CVC)** in 1964 as the apex body to oversee vigilance administration.

This committee is a landmark in the history of Indian administration because it institutionalized mechanisms to combat graft and maintain integrity among public servants.

Regarding the other options:
* **1953** is associated with the appointment of the first Backward Classes Commission (Kalelkar Commission).
* **1966** saw the creation of the first Administrative Reforms Commission (ARC).
* **1977** is linked to the appointment of the Ashok Mehta Committee on Panchayati Raj institutions.

Therefore, the correct year of appointment for the Santhanam Committee is **1962**.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: Who was the first Central Vigilance Commissioner of India?
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct answer is **Nittoor Srinivasa Rao**.

The **Central Vigilance Commission (CVC)** was established in 1964 based on the recommendations of the **Santhanam Committee** on Prevention of Corruption. Its primary role is to monitor all vigilance activities under the Central Government.

**Nittoor Srinivasa Rao** served as the first **Central Vigilance Commissioner** from 1964 to 1966. He was a distinguished jurist who played a pivotal role in laying the foundation for India's anti-corruption institutional framework.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:

* **S.A. Venkataraman** was a prominent civil servant but did not hold this specific position.
* **Malala Yousafzai** is a globally renowned activist for female education and the youngest Nobel Prize laureate; she is not associated with the Indian administrative system.
* **R.P. Sethupillai** was a famous Tamil scholar and writer, known for his contributions to Tamil literature, not for government vigilance roles.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: The Headquarters of central vigilance commission of india is at __________
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct answer is **Delhi**.

The **Central Vigilance Commission (CVC)** is the apex Indian governmental body established to address governmental corruption.

It was set up in **1964** based on the recommendations of the **K. Santhanam Committee**. The commission is headquartered in **New Delhi**, as it serves as the central agency for monitoring vigilance activities in the central government and various other organizations.

* **Chennai**, **Mumbai**, and **Pune** are major cities in India, but they do not serve as the seat of this national constitutional-status body.
* The CVC was granted statutory status in **2003** by an Act of Parliament, further cementing its role in overseeing integrity and transparency at the national level.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: Expand CVO
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct expansion of **CVO** is **Chief Vigilance Officer**.

**Chief Vigilance Officers** act as the principal advisors to the head of an organization in all matters concerning vigilance. They function as an extended arm of the **Central Vigilance Commission (CVC)**.

Here is why the other options are incorrect:
*   **Central Vigilance Officer** is a common misnomer, but the official designation used in all government departments and public sector undertakings is **Chief**.
*   **Central Veteran Officer** and **Chief Vigilance Organizer** are incorrect terms that do not correspond to the administrative structure of the Indian government.

The **CVO** is responsible for investigating complaints, conducting inspections, and ensuring transparency and integrity within their respective organizations. They play a critical role in preventing corruption and maintaining ethical standards in public service.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: Expand CTE
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct expansion for **CTE** in the context of government administration and vigilance is **Chief Technical Examiner**.

This organization functions under the **Central Vigilance Commission (CVC)** of India. Its primary role is to provide technical advice and support to the Commission regarding vigilance cases.

The **CTE Organization** (CTEO) is responsible for conducting technical audits of civil, electrical, and other works undertaken by various central government departments and public sector undertakings.

The acronym is often confused, but it specifically refers to the role of a **Chief Technical Examiner** who monitors large-scale projects to prevent corruption and ensure quality standards are maintained.

Option 2 is incorrect as it refers to entrepreneurship, which does not align with the administrative functions associated with this specific government designation.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: Expand CDI
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The term **CDI** in the context of administrative and disciplinary procedures in India stands for **Commissioners for Departmental Inquiries**.

These officials are appointed by the **Central Vigilance Commission (CVC)** to conduct departmental inquiries against public servants.

Here is a breakdown of why this is the correct expansion:

*   **Role**: They act as an inquiry authority to conduct oral inquiries into charges of misconduct against gazetted officers.
*   **Function**: Their primary goal is to ensure fair and impartial investigations into disciplinary cases, upholding the principles of natural justice.
*   **Significance**: By functioning as an independent inquiry body, they assist the disciplinary authorities in making informed decisions regarding administrative charges.

The other options are incorrect because they misidentify the function of the commissioners. The term is specifically linked to **disciplinary proceedings** rather than committees, conventions, or inequalities.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: The CBI Director in 2022 was __________
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct answer is **Subodh Kumar Jaiswal**.

In 2022, the **Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI)** was headed by **Subodh Kumar Jaiswal**. He is a 1985-batch **Indian Police Service (IPS)** officer belonging to the Maharashtra cadre.

He assumed the charge as the **Director of the CBI** on May 26, 2021, and served in this capacity throughout the year 2022.

Before his appointment as the CBI Director, he served as the **Director General of the Central Industrial Security Force (CISF)** and was also the **Director General of Police (DGP)** for the state of Maharashtra.

The other names listed, such as Rinku Naresh or Shivan Kumar, are not associated with the leadership of the CBI during this period, making them incorrect choices.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: Tenure of CBI director is how many years?
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct answer is **2 years**.

The **Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI)** Director serves a minimum tenure of two years as per the **Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946**.

This fixed tenure was established by the Supreme Court in the **Vineet Narain case (1997)** to ensure the operational independence of the agency and protect the Director from political interference.

In recent years, the government amended the law to allow for the extension of the Director's tenure. Under the new provisions, the term can be extended for up to **one year at a time**, provided the total tenure does not exceed **five years**.

These extensions are granted in the public interest, subject to the recommendations of a high-level committee. Despite these provisions for extension, the statutory minimum remains two years.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: Delhi special police establishment act was amended in which year?
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The **Delhi Special Police Establishment (DSPE) Act, 1946**, governs the functioning of the **Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI)**.

The significant amendment mentioned in the option refers to the **Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013**, which came into effect in **2014**.

Here is why this amendment is crucial:

*   The **2014 amendment** to the DSPE Act introduced changes to the **selection process** for the **Director of the CBI**.
*   It established a **High-Level Committee** responsible for recommending the appointment of the CBI Director.
*   The committee consists of the **Prime Minister** (Chairperson), the **Leader of the Opposition** (or the leader of the single largest opposition party), and the **Chief Justice of India** (or a Supreme Court Judge nominated by them).

This legislative change was introduced to ensure the independence of the CBI and to bring transparency to the appointment process of its head. While the Act has undergone various updates, the 2014 amendment remains a landmark transformation in the context of investigative autonomy in India.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: What is the Motto of the CBI?
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The motto of the **Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI)** is **Industry, Impartiality, and Integrity**.

These three principles serve as the guiding pillars for the agency's functioning and organizational ethos:

*   **Industry**: Represents the dedication, hard work, and diligence required to investigate complex criminal cases thoroughly.
*   **Impartiality**: Signifies the commitment to conducting investigations fairly, objectively, and without bias or external influence.
*   **Integrity**: Reflects the high moral standards and honesty expected from every officer to maintain public trust in the institution.

Since all three terms are integral to the official motto, option 3 is the correct choice. The **CBI** operates under the jurisdiction of the **Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions** and serves as India's premier investigative police agency.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: Which country is one of the largest republic countries?
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct answer is **India**.

A **republic** is a form of government where the country is considered a "public matter" and the head of state is usually an elected official rather than a monarch.

**India** is the world's largest democracy and a sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic **republic**. It gained its status as a republic on January 26, 1950, when its **Constitution** came into force.

Here is why the other options do not fit this description:

* **Sweden**: This is a **constitutional monarchy**. While it is a democratic state, the head of state is a monarch (the King), not an elected president.
* **New Zealand**: This is also a **constitutional monarchy**. The British monarch serves as the head of state, represented by a Governor-General.
* **Australia**: Similar to New Zealand, Australia operates as a **constitutional monarchy** under the British Crown.

In terms of population and administrative scale, **India** is significantly larger than the other nations listed, solidifying its position as one of the largest republics globally.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: Who is the main investigating agency of the central government?
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
The correct answer is the **Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI)**.

The **CBI** serves as the primary **investigating agency** of the central government in India. It functions under the jurisdiction of the **Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions** and is tasked with investigating major crimes like high-level corruption, economic offenses, and serious organized crime.

Here is why the other options are excluded:

* **CVC (Central Vigilance Commission):** This is an **advisory and supervisory body**, not an investigating agency. While it oversees vigilance administration, it refers corruption cases to the CBI or departmental authorities for investigation.
* **CPCR (Commission for Protection of Child Rights):** This body is specifically mandated to protect and promote the **rights of children**, rather than acting as a general criminal investigation agency for the government.

The **CBI** was established in 1963 based on the recommendations of the **Santhanam Committee** on Prevention of Corruption. It operates under the **Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946**, which grants it the legal authority to investigate offenses notified by the central government.

questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.q: Code and criminal procedure act was passed in which year?
questions/tm-polity-anti-corruption-meas.explanation:
